#6703. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6701. 5 Expert Habits to Find Inner Peace From Best-Selling Author Yung Pueblo

This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.

Yung Pueblo wants to be clear on something: “I’m not a monk.” Sure, in his lifetime he’s meditated for over 13,000 hours, but he still enjoys the drama and chaos of Love Island UK like the rest of us. The best-selling author’s philosophical thoughts on self-awareness, emotional healing, and mindfulness have reached over 3.5 million followers since he first started posting to Instagram in 2013. His digital presence has since grown into published works of poetry and prose, including the New York Times bestsellers Inward, Clarity & Connection, and The Way Forward. Now Pueblo, whose real name is Diego Perez, is releasing a new book: Journey: The Year That Changes Everything (Penguin Random House), a 365-day guide to finding inner peace.

What exactly is inner peace to Perez? “It means that you have a good relationship with your emotions,” he says. “It’s that you’re able to feel your emotions without necessarily fueling the heavy ones.”

Inner peace, per Perez, isn’t a final destination. It’s about recognizing negative feelings and using tools you’ve learned to acknowledge that they’re happening without allowing them to take over your life. That’s what Journey—which debuts on November 10—is about. The following habits are just a few of the techniques he’s developed to do exactly that. Below, Perez explains the creative benefits of walking, the value of daily gratitude, and why you should protect your own peace even when others around you are chaotic—the latter of which makes keeping up with reality TV that much more enjoyable.

Yung Pueblo: “Oftentimes we have a relationship where we’re afraid of change and we need to realize that the universe that we live in, it’s totally founded on change at every level of existence—the atomic level, the biological level, the cosmological level. It’s because of change that we even have the opportunity to experience things. If our universe was static, we wouldn’t be having this conversation right now. So changing our relationship with impermanence and making it one where we actually get inspired to be more present. When we’re with our friends, with our family, with your mom, with your dad, you know that they’re not always going to be around. So the times when you are with them, to be ever more present, because you know change will happen at one point or another. Being able to have that presence just makes you have this ability to really enjoy some of the most beautiful parts of life.

“When it’s a sad moment, you have to be like, ‘OK, this is not going to last forever.’ But also in the precious moments, this isn’t going to last forever, so let me be here in the moment.

“Another way to look at it is that it’s defined by your relationship with change. So the more that you’re able to embrace change and flow with change, then your mind’s going to have less stress. But it’s probably one of the biggest challenges any human being can accept— willingly trying to change their relationship with change.”

“So much of our impulsiveness just comes from these lightning-quick reactions that we think are our nature. We think that they’re unchangeable, but the reality is that we can train ourselves to slow down to be able to ask: OK, is this me having an impulsive reaction right now? and then asking ourselves: Is this actually useful? Should I act this out or instead should I actually choose something that’s different than what I would’ve done in the past? And in the act of slowing down and being intentional, you just end up finding way better results. This is a real habit. You can learn that from meditating, you can learn that from therapy, but you can also just teach yourself the raw skill of feeling impulsiveness coming up and then challenging yourself to slow down.

“I’m not going to jump to conclusions. I’m not going to say anything right now. Let me just check in with how I feel, what actually feels true to me, and then put forward something that I think is actually going to be helpful as opposed to just something that I later regret.

“So if a friend of yours is telling you about something that they’re really mad about, they’re offering an invitation for you to be angry with them on their behalf. But instead I found that I don’t necessarily want to be angry, but I want to be able to hear my friends and offer support or a listening ear or whatever the situation is needed. At the same time, I can remain in my own energy while offering support to this individual. We get sucked into the energy of other people really, really quickly, but instead of getting sucked into someone’s chaos, for the past two years, what I’ve been working on is: Can I live in my peace and offer my peace as an invitation? They can join me in my peace too, if they want to, instead of me just getting sucked into their drama.”

“We fall into self-analysis when we don’t feel good. It’s just the worst time for you to be analyzing yourself about what you’ve done right, what you’ve done wrong. Negative self-talk isn’t productive. It’s good for you to be honest with yourself, but honesty also can come with gentleness and with self-acceptance. But when your mood is low, it’s going to be really hard for you to be gentle with yourself. So one thing I realize is when I don’t feel good or I’m over-exhausted from too much work or too much travel or whatnot, that’s the time for me to just suspend self-analysis and just treat myself gently—be mindful of what I’m saying to other people too, and just let it pass.

“And in the act of letting it pass, then you can do some more proper self-assessment because your best assessment is going to be when your mind is calm, not when it’s heavy.”

“Life is a long series of ups and downs, and there’s nothing wrong with that. But in the down moments, we tend to look at everything with such darkness that we forget that we still have access to clean water, that we still have access to food, that we have a house over our head. A lot of people in the world don’t have that. Having gratitude for the basics and the fundamentals really helps reset the balance where if something went wrong at work, you’re going to be okay, you’re going to be fine.”

“This is my recent favorite and it’s the newest habit that I picked up. You got to walk. You got to go for walks. Walking supports clarity, and I think it really supports creativity. I find that whenever I feel a little stuck with writing, just going on a 20- or 40-minute walk really helps to regenerate and create this new sense of clarity.”

#6699. CBK Lovers, Take Note: The ’90s Heeled Loafer Is Making a Comeback

There’s a photo of Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. leaving the Bowery Bar in October of 1995—it’s blurry and grainy and because of it, one of CBK’s lesser known style references. Still, it lives in my mind for a particular reason: her shoes. In the image, she’s wearing a white button-down and cropped, flared jeans with a pair of Prada 1995 heeled Dalmatian-print loafers. It’s this exact photograph that sparked in me an early fascination with Bessette-Kennedy’s footwear, and prompted a year-long hunt to source the rare shoe styles she wore in the nineties. I’ve yet to uncover this specific animal-printed pair on the secondhand market (rest assured, my notifications are set); I’d argue it might be one of her hardest to track down.

The spotted print first appeared on Prada’s fall 1995 runway in heeled-mule form (later seen on Kate Moss in the summer of 1996). While Bessette-Kennedy’s heeled loafers are my white whale, the silhouette feels just as relevant today. To wit: Earlier this fall, Prada reissued its coveted Dalmatian-print loafers; elsewhere Herbert Levine, Dries Van Noten, and Phoebe Philo all offered their own interpretations of the shoe trend for the season.

For me, part of the heeled loafer’s appeal in the ’90s was the balance it struck between masculine and feminine dressing—the substantial upper of a traditional loafer lifted by a heel. From Kate Moss at the airport to Gwyneth Paltrow on the red carpet, the shoe earned its reputation as one of the most versatile styles of the decade—a sentiment that still rings true. Worn with jeans and a white tee, or a slouchy knit and tailored trouser, the heeled loafer possesses just enough structure and height to balance casual day wear with a touch of sophistication.

While I remain on the hunt for an elusive original Prada, these are the current styles that I’d invest in, each getting something right about the heeled ’90s loafer.

While most of us equate the fashion in the ’90s as minimalist, some of the decade’s boldest prints appeared on its shoes. The printed loafer came into its own in those years, when Miuccia Prada and Tom Ford at Gucci invigorated the traditionally staid shape, turning out punchy options in brightly colored snakeskin and animal-print pony hair. Prada’s 1995 spotted loafer is one of my favorite examples, and the modern reissue possesses all the charm of the original. (Keep an eye out for Dries’s SS27 collection—which was filled with bold printed pairs.) When styling this kind of shoe, I like to keep the rest of my look simple, letting a glimpse of the pattern peek out from beneath a pair of worn-in Levi’s or even a black tailored trouser.

A more casual take on the heeled loafer is the mule—seen in the mid-nineties on the runways, on the red carpet, and even at the airport. With Saint Laurent and JW Anderson among the brands revisiting the shape today, I’d take my styling cue from Moss and play up a punchy pattern with a white Leset tee and some cropped High Sport trousers.

Among the heeled loafers that took off in the ’90s, the minimalist version had a distinctly off-duty ease. From the Row’s modern shape, to sharp takes by Khaite, the minimalist loafer is equal parts understated and refined. I am perpetually on the hunt for a loafer that I can wear with anything from a good jean to a slip dress, and this is exactly that. In colder months, I look for pairs with a little give to their leather so there’s room for a thicker sock.

#6698. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6697. John Legend, Lynn Nottage, and Whitney White on Reclaiming an American Classic From a Black Perspective

The three artists have teamed up on a musical adaptation of Imitation of Life

In 2020, against the dual backdrops of the isolating Covid-19 lockdown and the righteous fury of Black Lives Matter protests erupting across the country, John Legend and Lynn Nottage began exchanging messages. Though the EGOT-achieving musician and the two-time Pulitzer Prize–winning playwright couldn’t meet in person, the pair quietly became collaborators on a long-gestating project, now finally reaching the stage: a musical adaptation of Imitation of Life.

For nearly a century, Imitation of Life—which began as a 1933 best-selling novel by Fannie Hurst, became a John M. Stahl melodrama the following year, then was adapted for the screen again by Douglas Sirk in 1959—has been a cinematic fixture in Black American households, though not an uncontroversial one. Stahl’s iconic telling centers on Bea Pullman, a white widow and single mother, who takes in Delilah, a Black single mother, as a maid in exchange for housing her and her light-skinned daughter, Peola (Sarah Jane in Sirk’s version). When Bea boxes Delilah’s family pancake recipe and puts a caricature of her likeness on the package—an unmistakable nod to Aunt Jemima—she becomes a wealthy businesswoman. But Delilah, content simply to care for Bea and her daughter, turns down any share of the money. Meanwhile, Peola, seduced by her adjacency to whiteness, wrenchingly disavows her mother to pursue a life of passing.

As Sterling Brown’s scathing and influential 1935 review for Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life made plain, the novel and film are mired in racist tropes. Yet despite its flaws, the story has continued capturing Black audiences, perhaps for the complex humanity clearly latent within Delilah’s and Peola’s characters. Now the story is being retold in a limited-run production opening December 3 at the Shed in New York, this time with a fully realized Delilah as the lead and an all-Black chief creative team at its core. Nottage wrote the book, while Legend—who also recently released his 11th studio album, Muse—composed the entire score. Whitney White, of Jaja’s African Hair Braiding and Liberation, directs, with Adrienne Warren starring as Delilah and Jessica Vosk as Bea. Leading up to rehearsals for the show, Nottage, Legend, and White—so in demand that she was pulled into a production meeting midconversation—took time to discuss their own relationships to Imitation of Life, their experience working together, and why the story’s themes remain as relevant as ever.

Lynn Nottage: I come from a generation where both films, Imitation of Life from the 1930s and 1950s, were fairly ubiquitous on television. I ended up seeing the films probably once or twice a year and found myself in sort of a tense, love-hate relationship with Imitation of Life, in that I was frustrated by the treatment of Delilah and Peola in 1934, then once again by Delilah and Sarah Jane in the 1950s. And yet I was fascinated by the racial politics and this young woman who had a really angsty relationship with her own identity. So I felt, when I was invited to work on this, that I had an opportunity to delve deeper into the character of Delilah and right some wrongs. She is so fascinating; she’s a mother, she’s an entrepreneur, she’s a woman who defies the expectations of the time. And yet throughout history, she has not been given her just deserts.

John Legend: I didn’t grow up knowing this film, but my parents and their generation know it very well. So when I told them that I was involved in this musical, they were so excited. And it made me realize how important this work was in our culture. But like Lynn, it was a fun challenge to reimagine the storytelling, where Delilah was centered, her emotionality was centered, her humanity was centered, and Peola’s humanity was centered as well.

And then, of course, I’ve never written a musical before. So part of the joy and educational experience that I’ve gotten from doing this is working with people who have so much brilliance and experience and understanding of a medium that I didn’t bring to the table. It was the perfect introduction, for me, to writing a musical. It’s been such a welcoming and edifying way to enter into this new branch of my career.

Nottage: John is a natural in this medium. It’s almost as if he had gotten a master’s degree in musical-theater writing. I think that, John, you have so many musicals in you and the world is going to be blown away.

Legend: Thank you. It really did make me think, why hadn’t I done this before?

Whitney White: For me, I was raised by a single mom, and she raised me at great personal cost—spiritual cost—in Chicago, on her own. So the 1930s film, I oddly was more familiar with it because I liked it more. I would sit with my grandmother when she was having her coffee, like, at whatever-o’clock in the morning, because neither of us would ever sleep. And for some reason, I attached myself to the 1930s film. The visuals of that film are so iconic. It’s like the foundation of Americana as it exists in global culture is visualized in that film. But also the story of Delilah echoes in so many ways. It’s almost like touching a stove that’s too hot for me. Because I’ve watched, my whole life, the world not see my mother in this way: her brilliance, her intelligence, her spunk, her grit. So I just knew that I could bring something to it. But I also knew that John and Lynn were going to give that character the eulogy and the eternal life that she’s always deserved.

Legend: Yeah, I think because of Lynn’s perspective and storytelling, we see other sides of Delilah. We see her being romantic. We see her being a brilliant businessperson, making a way out of no way—something that a lot of our ancestors, especially, had to do. They did what they had to do to realize the American dream.

Nottage: At the core, this is a story about the American dream, with all of its contradictions and complications. It’s a story about motherhood; it’s a story about friendship, but it’s also a story about passing. It’s what we are forced to do to negotiate and survive in a world that is sexist, in a world that is racist. Why, in America, do we constantly have to make compromises in order to reach for the things that we desire? Those sacrifices, most often, people of color have to make, women have to make. We are often asked to reshape our identities to fit into some sort of template that’s not necessarily comfortable for the shapes and forms of our bodies and our ideas and our identities. I think that’s why we keep coming back to this story, because the struggle remains real.

White: And I think, in the midst of having to constantly reshape our identities and bodies as Black folk, at the same time, we got the goods. We make culture. Here you have this character who saves this business, and what does she make? Delicious food that is worth millions of dollars. So while we’re forced to be at the bottom of the totem pole, we also make the goods that make capitalism work. That’s something I’ve really been sitting with: We’re so often plundered and taken from the most, and yet we are the foundation of capitalism.

Nottage: Can I ask you, Whitney, you’re looking particularly luminous today. Where are you going?

White: Girl, I’m sweaty. I just walked my child [to school]. My child is very heavy. I have this giant toddler; maybe he’s going to be LeBron. He didn’t want to walk to school, so he made me push him in his stroller.

Legend: I met your husband last week, so I see where he got it from.

Nottage: I totally digress, but I was like, “Look at you, you have, like, a rosy green glow.” [Laughs]

White: [Laughs] That beat that just happened is so beautiful because it’s so indicative of the show. Like, we’re talking about this heavy stuff, and then we all have this beautiful laugh. When I read the text and hear the music, it’s like I go through 10 cycles of emotions. I laugh, I cry, I fall in love, then I laugh and cry and fall in love again.

Legend: One of my favorite things from the workshops is watching the music come to life. You have all these amazing performers embodying all the things that I wrote in my little piano room at home.

Nottage: Theater is often so difficult and fraught to make because it is collaborative. I think one of the things that’s been really lovely about this process is the ease with which we, as collaborators, are capable of having conversations, because there’s so much mutual respect and appreciation. The bottom line in making a musical is that trust is necessary. It’s a tremendous leap of faith.

White [as she is pulled into production meeting]: I just want to add one last thing. Oh God, I don’t want to get too emotional. Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine that I would be sitting here with two of my favorite living artists. When I started in this business, this kind of makeup for a musical team was impossible. I can’t tell you how much pride and excitement that brings me, to be working alongside John and Lynn.

Nottage: Thank you. We love you, Whitney.

White: I’m going to go lovingly yell at people—lovingly, lovingly. Bye.

Legend: Our writing process started—we were meeting during Covid, so a lot of our first interactions were on Zoom. Lynn would send me pages with story dialogue and possible lyrical ideas. I would sit in my piano room and sketch out an idea with maybe a couple lyrics, but mostly just mumbling musical ideas around the theme.

Legend: One of the things that happens more in musical theater than I’m used to is the revision process and the workshopping process. … I’ve definitely done more revision in this show than I’ve ever done in my pop-music career.

Nottage: John, do you remember one of the very first conversations that we had? I said, “We’re probably going to write that opening-number song at least 15 times.” You’re like, “Oh, I don’t think so.” Here we are!

Legend: Here we are. We’ve rewritten it multiple times. [Laughs] I don’t have an extensive knowledge bank of musicals that I’ve seen and been a part of. So it was interesting, thinking about how to write for one, because part of it was like, “Well, let me just bring my own musical experience in the church and popular music and, you know, singing in a jazz a cappella group and singing show tunes in the choir in high school.” I just brought my own experience and said, “Let me just write the songs that I can be proud of and that I believe will work.” And then Lynn really taught me how to incorporate the storytelling into the songs.

Nottage: It’s so interesting to hear you say that, John, because I think one of the things that made the process so smooth is that you are a natural-born storyteller. There’s something that you understand instinctively and fundamentally about dramaturgy that I didn’t have to explain to you. I would venture to say that perhaps musicals are the hardest form of theater-making just because it is so layered.

But I also want to circle back to something that you said earlier, John, about the beginning of the process. It was Covid, and we were all thinking and making in isolation. There was something really lovely about reaching across the country to John and having these conversations about a book, even though we didn’t really, at that point, know each other. We spent a lot of time talking about ideas. It was absolutely thrilling. When I got that first mumble, I was like, “Oh my God, it’s John Legend mumbling, and it still sounds beautiful.” It was a song that we never, ultimately, ended up using. I think that eventually you should do an album of the outtakes.

Nottage: I just want to add, because we’ve been talking about some heavy themes, that the musical is not delivering spinach. The musical embodies all of the complexities of a beautiful woman like Delilah, a beautiful woman like Bea, a beautiful woman like Peola. It really is, in some ways, a celebration. It is a love letter. And it is a gift to be able to be in dialogue with these women.

#6695. Why This 251-Year-Old Watchmaker Is Suddenly Hotter Than Ever in 2026

Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.

Founded in the late 18th century by perhaps the world’s most famous watchmaker, Abraham Louis-Breguet, the eponymous brand was once the horologer to royalty. (He famously made a watch for Marie Antoinette that she unfortunately, ahem, never got the chance to wear.) Breguet is responsible for the tourbillon, an early self-winding mechanism, his famous namesake numerals that nearly every brand in Switzerland uses now, and much more. But despite its massive contributions to horology, the brand's pieces haven't caused frenzies among collectors like those from Rolex, Patek Philippe, or even Cartier. However, like Dune’s Bene Gesserit, the watchmaker’s plans are apparently measured in centuries. Recent signals point to the idea that Breguet may be entering a new golden era as collectors come around to its exquisitely made timepieces.

Follow the money, and you’ll quickly find evidence of Breguet’s glow-up. Late last month, at Monaco Legends Group’s fall watch auction, a 1970s-era piece previously owned by a 50-year veteran Breguet watchmaker sold for €221,000. That was nearly of the beginning of the brand's impressive run of auction that makes us wonder, What’s going on with Breguet these days?

Abraham Louis-Breguet isn’t the only hallowed watchmaker to steer the brand. Legendary names like George Daniels, F.P. Journe, and Michel Parmigiani have contributed to the brand’s legacy. At auction, many collectors are keying in on a period of Breguet led by Daniel Roth from the mid-’70s to 1987. After he left Breguet, Roth went on to found his own successful brand that now sells for six figures at auction. The combination of these two powers is proving irresistible to today’s collectors.

The Ref. 3050A was a signature piece of Roth’s reign at Breguet and epitomizes the designer’s contributions to the brand. Roth introduced the first modern piece from the manufacturer with a perpetual calendar. The piece’s guilloché dial is also a signature of the Roth era. The watch sold for €85,800 at the end of October.

The 3057 was the successor to Roth’s first watch at Breguet, the 3050. The big change is the transparent caseback. This lovely semi-skeletonized perpetual calendar hammered for some 200% above its estimate—not a huge surprise considering Breguet made only a couple of these a year when they were in production. Notably, thanks to the addition of that exhibition caseback, we can see the pretty, highly decorated automatic movement.

It’s platinum. It’s skeletonized. It’s got a tourbillon. It’s got a matching bracelet. It’s accompanied by all its factory goodies. What else could one ask for in a pre-owned Breguet? Still, a $387,000 hammer price is a remarkable outcome.

Classique Grandes Complications ref. 5447

This oversized perpetual-calendar minute repeater, likewise executed in platinum, commanded almost $271,000 at Phillips this weekend—proof positive of the appeal of classical Breguet looks mixed with modern movement technology and finishing.

An evolution of the Daniel Roth-era ref. 3350, this gorgeous tourbillon wristwatch features one of the hallmarks of Breguet’s signature style: a beautifully guilloché dial combined with blued steel hands and a Roman-numeral minute track.

Breguet took a significant left turn in the 1950s when it began producing the Type XX flyback chronograph for French military aviators. It still serves as an important pillar in the brand’s lineup today.

Introduced in the late 1980s, the ref. 3350 is Breguet’s first wrist-worn tourbillon—a significant milestone for the brand that invented the complication. Emblematic of the Daniel Roth era of Breguet production, it has since become a neo-vintage classic.

Released in 2025 in celebration of the firm’s 250th birthday, the Classique Souscription uses a single hand to tell the time against a Grand Feu enamel dial mirroring vintage Breguet pocket watches. Just this week, the maison followed it up with the platinum version seen above.

The Expérimentale 1 is the first step in a new collection of envelope-pushing, ultra-complicated watches. Fitted with advanced materials, the “1” features watchmaking’s very first high-frequency tourbillon, which beats at an astounding 10 Hz. This is a great way forward for modern Breguet—a model that embraces the brand’s tradition as the industry's most inventive watchmaker.

Now a quarter-millennium old, Breguet has one of the most extensive histories of any watchmaker still in operation, with records reaching back generations. Its finishing is exceptional; its complications are rooted in some of the earliest experiments by one of the world’s most famous horologists; and its designs are superb. As prices continue to skyrocket for watches at auction, especially for hotshot newcomers, it’s exciting to see one of the most storied brands in history catch fire, too.

#6694. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6693. I Love a Famous Man With Nice Things to Say About His Ex

I’m the first to admit that I have somewhat nontraditional taste in men. An impressive and well-paid job? Ugh. Give me a freelance drummer any day! Yet the thing that possibly attracts me most isn’t their looks or their earning potential; rather, it’s their dynamic with their ex-partners.

As the daughter of parents who worked hard to remain positive about one another after their divorce, it may not be entirely surprising that I’m insanely into men who only have good things to say about their former spouses. Ben Affleck and Jennifer Lopez are frequently held up as an ideal of friendship after romantic entanglement; random old photos of them hanging out post-split frequently go viral on social media to this day. But hearing Affleck praise Lopez—as well as his ex-wife and co-parent Jennifer Garner—in a recent interview only served to revive my insane crush on him, giant phoenix back tattoo and all.

“To understand Jennifer Lopez, honestly, is to understand somebody who really is a pioneer, who did things when she was told they’re not possible and you’re not welcome, by [a] kind of force of will,” Affleck recently told Jorge and Paola Ramos on their podcast The Moment, going on to call Lopez “probably the hardest-working person that I’ve ever known.”

The thing that’s hot to me here isn’t just Affleck’s obvious respect for Lopez—it’s his specificity. Instead of just heaping empty platitudes upon his ex, he’s going out of his way to spotlight her ambition and professional tenacity.

And though I raised my eyebrow at Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin’s “conscious uncoupling” just as much as the next Goop skeptic, I have to admit that their bond remains inspiring to me nonetheless. Paltrow and Martin are parents to 22-year-old Apple and 20-year-old Moses, and I loved Paltrow’s summary of her relationship with Martin in 2015, just months after she filed for divorce: “It’s been hard, and we’ve gone through really difficult times, but we’ve always said these children are our priority. What that really means is, even though today you hate me and you never want to see me again, we’re going to brunch because it’s Sunday and that’s what we're going to do.”

I don’t have kids with my own ex, but we do share a reactive Maltipoo rescue. If people like Paltrow and Martin or Courteney Cox and David Arquette—the parents to 22-year-old Coco—have managed to transform their former romantic relationship into something more polite and familial, why can’t we?

As if I needed any more reason to lust pathetically after Lenny Kravitz, he referred to his own ex-wife Lisa Bonet as “the most beautiful woman on the planet” (I mean, yeah!) in 2024, adding: “The love doesn’t leave you, but it has to find a new way to funnel itself into a new life. We consciously wanted to do that. It took time, believe me, but she is a part of my life that will never leave my heart, my soul or my spirit. I am what I am because of our experience.” Why is this breakup ode literally more romantic and poignant than any mid-relationship love letter I’ve ever received?

Of course, beware the man—celebrity or not—who’s too into his ex; unfinished business can really put a crimp in your future plans, whether he acknowledges it or not. But if you really want to know what a guy is like underneath the veneer of new-relationship energy, pay close attention to how he talks about his exes. If he’s rude or disrespectful about them, hit the bricks—but if he’s polite and fond, feel free to consider that among the very greenest of greeen lights.

#6691. Why Blake Griffin Couldn’t Leave Basketball Alone

Twelve years ago, I was sitting in Blake Griffin’s house, listening to him tell me that under no circumstances would he stay around basketball after he retired. “Well, look who’s a liar,” he says now.

Griffin is a former NBA All-Star who played for 14 years, many of them for the Clippers, before announcing his retirement in 2024. He now has his own show, The Stepback with Blake Griffin, and a weekly gig with NBA on Prime, as part of their studio show. “I always thought that there was a little bit too much negativity when it came to scrutinizing players,” Griffin says. “This is a job that 400-something guys have. It’s extremely hard. I don’t need to go on TV and I don’t need to tell everybody that the guy that went three for 17 sucks at basketball. He doesn’t.”

On The Stepback, Griffin puts on a suit, sits behind a desk, and addresses a big, sports-related topic each week: the media, taxpayer-financed stadiums, the rocketing costs of youth sports, and so on. Like him, the show is unexpectedly funny, frequently insightful, and a good hang. In this conversation, he and I discuss the Clippers then and now, retiring at 34, and what it was like to have some rude journalist visit his house, all those years ago.

The following conversation is lightly edited and condensed from the latest episode of One More Question with Zach Baron. Watch below or on YouTube. Listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

Blake Griffin: It’s funny, being 37 now, looking back at that time, and being like: “Man, I didn’t know what I was doing.” I can’t believe people were entrusting me with having a house and a car and doing all these adult things. I wasn’t an adult yet.

Well, in fairness to me, I’d only been living there for four years—no, I think it was fairly new at the time. I moved into that house at the end of 2013 and we spoke the next year. So over time you collect more stuff, figure out your taste.

He walked me through the entire party for—it felt like an hour, I don’t know, I had lost track of time. When you’re holding a 70-something-year-old man’s hand who’s not related to you, being introduced to party guests—and I think I was 19 at the time, I’d just gotten drafted—time sort of slows down. So I don’t know how long it was. Could have been half a day. But yeah, from the first time I met him, it was a very different experience.

Everybody, when I first moved there, was like, “Where are you from?” I’m like, “From Oklahoma.” And they’re like, “Oh, so—horses?” I’m like, “Well, yeah, but also cars.” It’s a civilized place. Culture shock in just that—I didn’t live in Hollywood, but you’re just in LA and that’s the epicenter of so much. It was a lot, but also you’re so focused when you’re 19. Apartment, practice facility, airport—those are the three things that I did. So it kind of gave me time to grow up. And then when we met, I was a much more seasoned man at 24, 25. It’s crazy looking back, because you’re like, “Man, I can’t believe I moved there at 19.” I tell people all the time, I grew up in LA.

I didn’t really dwell on that question. I don’t know. It was cool. I really enjoyed our conversation.

No, it’s fine. I was going there on my own. It’s fine. I’m happy to give one. I did. I enjoyed our conversation. I was actually thinking about it on the way here. Those are the best conversations—when you can just sit and talk and there’s not just these six questions that you’ve got to hit. You just let the conversation go where it goes. That’s what the conversation felt like to me.

Well, look who’s a liar. You know what’s crazy is, I never envisioned myself doing the NBA on Prime Show. And even until I retired and had conversations about going to join TNT or ESPN, whatever it was, and I still didn’t want to. And it really was Amazon getting a part of the TV rights and them really wanting to do a show differently than what was already on air. And that intrigued me because I thought there was this space in the NBA particularly where you can just analyze games, you can talk about basketball. And I always thought that there was a little bit too much negativity when it came to scrutinizing players. This is a job that 400 something guys have. It’s extremely hard. I don’t need to go on TV and I don’t need to tell everybody that the guy that went three for 17 sucks at basketball. He doesn’t. He had an off night. Instead, maybe I can walk you through some of the things he maybe could have done differently or some of the things he did well and it just wasn’t his night.

It’s kind of how I talk just in real life. I don’t want to harp on somebody who’s going through a shooting slump. Trust me, no one in the world wants to shoot better than the guy who’s in a shooting slump. It happened to me. Trust me. So I don’t need to come on TV and talk about it. So it’s kind of the same way I talk to people just in real life about certain games or what happened with this, what happened with that? It doesn’t always have to be negative.

I still do. I think that the day that I am bitter, or the day that I watch the game and I only see it from a negative standpoint or I’m like, “Back in our day, we didn’t do this or these guys are getting paid too much money”—I think that’s probably the day that I don’t need to do this anymore, because if I’m not going to adapt to where the game is today, I think that’s where you end up being jaded and you end up being biased in your observation or your analysis. And that’s what we’re hired to do, give our analysis. But it’s also like: Give your analysis on basketball today. It doesn’t matter what happened back then. And so my biggest thing too is every year I try to spend time with coaches, GMs, whoever it is, to keep understanding where the game is going, because it does change. Basketball evolves and you have to evolve your mindset around it.

We’re actually boys now. We went and did this golf thing together. I can’t lie. I was always just like, “What? Why? Give me a break, man.” I never was like, “Gosh, Charles is awesome.” Then you spend time with him and you see who he is and I appreciate it. I wasn’t the only person and at times it’s also not unwarranted. There’s games I played bad, I could have done better and this and that. And if that’s his style and that’s how he does it, that’s totally fine. It’s not that you can’t be critical. I just think I wanted to do [it] a little different.

There are definitely guys like that. My advice, if you’re in that spot, or something I wish somebody had told me when I was in this transition of really trying to develop my game, but also I was known for being aggressive, athletic, attack the rim, is you can continue to develop this skill and you continue to work on your game, but don’t go away from the things that got you to this place in the first place. So I would say to guys, use your athleticism, get to the rim, put pressure on the rim and then let that be your play making because now people have to rotate over, they have to help. Now you can open up different parts of your game. So a lot of times players hear all this like, “He can’t do this, he can’t do that.” And sometimes you kind of block out what you do well and you’re just so focused on what people are saying you can’t do.

Yeah. I mean, it’s almost impossible not to. I wouldn’t read tweets. I don’t read mentions during the season especially, but I wouldn’t put a lot of thought into comments, but it’s hard not to... When you’re just watching sports and you love watching sports and there’s morning shows on and it’s all around you, you’re going to hear stuff. And then there’s also the side of you that you know what you need to get better at as well.

I watched the game a little bit differently. I think as a player, I was watching so much of player tendencies, like I’m going to be guarding this guy in a couple days, or whatever it is. You’re also watching plays, you’re seeing teams run different sets. And now I’m interested a little bit more in the chess match that’s happening because trying to analyze, you’re looking at, okay, “What are the matchups? What would I have maybe done differently in that matchup? What could they do differently? What worked well? What didn’t work well?” And then you’re watching both sides of the ball, obviously. So it’s a lot of the same obviously basketball viewing, but I think when you’re trying to watch from an analyst perspective, you have to be a little bit more all-encompassing. When I’m watching as a player at night, if we don’t have a game, I’m not really tuning into, “Oh, since so-and-so got a tech, they’ve been on a 7-0 run,” but that’s something you clock now because it’s part of telling the story of the game.

I think it was my time. I think when I got to the point where I still enjoyed the game of basketball, but I was enjoying less and less everything else that came with it. My last several years I was in Detroit, I was in Brooklyn, I was in Boston, and my kids are in school in Los Angeles. So being away from them was tough. Even getting to see them once a month is still a little bit brutal. Or you’re on the road, you come back here, you get a couple days. So that wore on me. I also had an unfortunate amount of injuries, and I felt like I was having to put just as much in just to practice and then recover from that practice and then get ready for the game the next day, and it became this whole thing. I felt like I wanted to walk away from basketball on my own terms. I had a chance to go play another year and took some time to think about it, and I just felt like it was my time.

I don’t think there was a specific moment. I did remember when training camp came back around that next season and I was still trying to decide and I realized I didn’t feel like I was missing anything. I was like, “Oh, all right. Not as scary as I thought it would be.” Then as the season went on, I just didn’t see myself going back. I remember I was playing golf with JJ Redick once before I retired. This was before he took the job with the Lakers, and he said something to me that just stuck with me. He was like, “I’m telling you, you won’t be truly happy until you retire.” It kind of shocked me. Because he and I played together for five years, I think, and we were so similar in the way we prepared and the way we worked and how much we cared about the game that it just is this all-encompassing, obsessive thing. And it’s hard to really appreciate the little things, and it’s hard to appreciate making your own schedule. The school drop-offs, first day of school, doing all these different things. That’s sort of the way I took it, and the way I think that he meant it—is it’s such a grind, mental grind, physical grind, of putting literally everything you have into this thing. And then when you’re done, you just find this new sense of peace.

It’s amazing. I mean, I hope that they understood why I was having to be gone so much, but just being present is such a huge, huge gift. I mean, literally yesterday, my son had a football game that was two hours outside of LA. I drove two hours to watch an hour and a half football game, and then two hours back, and I was so happy. Now their games are what brings me sports joy.

It’s definitely scary because it’s also the one thing that you’ve done your whole life. And you also have to think—I dropped out of college. A lot of guys don’t even go, or guys are maybe there one year, and you don’t get the college experience of the workload and classes and graduating, internships, your first foray into the working world and you’re learning all these lessons and figuring out who you’re going to be, who you want to be, or how to operate in that world, and you miss out on that, and then you retire. I think a lot of guys have that What now? thing. And for me personally, doing nothing was never an option. I would be bored out of my mind. So that’s one thing I always preach to younger guys is find something you think you may want to do before you’re done.

Even in the offseason, you have to work out. So it’s still all based around this one thing. So even your free time is not quite necessarily like, “Okay, all right, go do whatever you want.” And then the season is so structured and you don’t really think about it. Every move is planned. You have your schedule in advance so you know it. It’s not like a surprise, but there’s no free time. I remember when I got traded to the Pistons, somebody asked me: “So, do you just commute? Are you still living in LA?” And I’m like, “No, no. We play every other day. There’s no commute time.”

You definitely have those moments. #6690. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6689. Does Influencer Gifting Still Work in the Algorithm Age?

Influencer gifting, once a savvy play, is now standard practice: on affiliate platform ShopMy, the typical brand now sends 350% more gifts a year than it did in 2022, while rival platform LTK’s annual study with Northwestern University found the average number of creators brands work with rose 275% in the past year.

But more product hasn’t necessarily meant more visibility. Algorithms now reward reach beyond a creator’s followers, affiliate platforms have made posting feel transactional, and access to A-listers increasingly runs through paid placements and a gatekept network of stylists.

That gifting has become an overplayed strategy is precisely the problem. “There has just become too much of it all: too much gifting, too much content, too many paid posts,” says celebrity stylist Dani Michelle, who styles It-girls including Kendall Jenner, Hailey Bieber, and Daisy Edgar-Jones. Tyra Booker, assistant VP of integrated marketing at Rare Beauty, says at a past job, she witnessed the earned media value (EMV) of send-outs falling. “It’s not that these mailers are bad,” she says. “It’s just that fewer people are opening them.” (EMV is the monetary value of brand publicity or exposure that is gained organically.)

Creators are also less willing to post for free. “There’s now a healthier amount of awareness around being paid to play,” Booker says, meaning brands can no longer simply send product and expect content in return. “If a brand requires a guaranteed post, that’s a paid partnership, not organic seeding,” says Jenine Leigh, managing partner at LA-based influencer and marketing agency The A List. That means without an agreement, gifted goods are more likely to just vanish into the abyss.

Affiliate platforms offer a middle ground. On sites like ShopMy and LTK, brands upload a curated selection of products, often called a gifting lookbook, and creators choose what they’d like to be sent. If a creator then shares the piece, they do so with a trackable link, earning commission on any sales it drives, so the brand can see exactly which posts convert. Creators have an incentive to post, too: beyond the commission, a strong track record on the platform helps brands identify the creators who actually drive sales, which, ShopMy’s marketing head Ivy Zhang says, means gifting starts to work more like a sales channel than a marketing expense.

Sophia Geiss is one influencer who has embraced affiliate platforms like LTK.

The algorithms have shifted, too. Reach increasingly comes from those who don’t follow a creator at all: follower growth is down, while non-follower views are up, as social strategist Rachel Karten notes in her newsletter, “Link in Bio”. “I hear from brands all the time that follower count doesn’t correlate with engagement, clicks or purchases,” Karten says.

If gifting is no longer the promised publicity — and sales — boost it once was, how should brands evolve their seeding strategies?

Unlike gifting, a paid placement is a contract: a brand pays a stylist to put a specific piece on a client. These deals are nothing new, but over the past three to five years, they’ve spread well beyond a select few brands, says one PR agency founder who brokers them, speaking anonymously. What’s changed is the pay-off. Brands can now repurpose the image and link it directly to their shops, and the shots they prefer are the ones that look unplanned, like an airport outfit or a coffee run, the founder says.

“Brands 100% want a photo of a celebrity papped wearing their outfit more than an editorial shot, because it feels like the celebrity chose to wear it, even if they didn’t,” they add. In an era where consumers are hyper-aware of brand deals, this approach offers at least an air of authenticity — even if, behind the scenes, the brand PRs are the ones coordinating with the paps.

An average A-list placement costs $25,000 to $30,000, rising to north of $50,000 for a top name — and that’s often for a single piece, such as a necklace, or a pair of shoes or sunglasses, which the stylist works into an outfit. The fee usually goes to the stylist rather than the celebrity, though one stylist, speaking anonymously, says she splits the fee with her client. Payment only happens once a piece is worn and documented. “You still cannot ultimately control if they’re going to wear it,” says the agency founder. “At the last minute, the celebrity could be like, ‘Nah, I’m not wearing that.’” If a piece doesn’t work for the look or the event, no money changes hands.

Other arrangements are murkier. “Sometimes, the brand just has a really good relationship with the stylist. They gift them a lot, a bit of cash changes hands [for paid placements],” says the agency founder. “It’s a little less ‘get that dress on’, and more ‘keep us around’.”

The price to play may have skyrocketed, but the exact return on a paid placement is hard to quantify. Still, the agency founder says placements can earn back their fee and more in direct sales, though they concede it’s “case by case”. One brand recently paid an extra $20,000 after running a placement image as an ad without the rights, and shrugged it off: “We made so much money off that image. Who cares?”

Not every brand can make the math work, though. “You need a significant budget for paid partnerships with VIPs these days,” says Julia Chalmers, founder of LA-based brand marketing and communications agency Lucky Chalm, and “often a brand won’t see the return from such a high investment.”

For brands that seed organically, such as Colleen Allen’s self-funded label, the return depends on timing. Gregory Mitola, founder of brand development and communications firm Etagere, held off on influencer gifting until the brand was stocked at Net-a-Porter and Moda Operandi. “We weren’t at major retailers, so it felt a bit premature,” he says. Instead, the label built awareness through intimate salon-style presentations and by dressing industry women it believed in, offering them friends-and-family pricing, “so they’re out and about wearing the brand.” Its first round of gifting, focused on the new Bustle Bag, went out in late October, and even now, it’s measured. Mitola gifted 15 people: eight celebrities, five influencers, and two industry professionals. “We’re not gifting up the wazoo,” he says.

Carey Mulligan in a Colleen Allen FW26 look.

For brands unwilling or unable to pay the big bucks for paid placements, they need to get savvy about how they seed. Rather than sending product to as many people as possible, the brands cutting through are now focusing on a handful of the right names. “Volume on its own isn’t what drives value anymore, it’s the precision,” says Alison Bringé, CMO at Launchmetrics. “The real advantage in seeding today comes from knowing which talent is creating measurable impact for your brand, and building your strategy around them.”

For Rare Beauty’s Booker, that means specificity: a new, targeted list for each launch, built around niche creators, such as the early-2000s nostalgia accounts she targeted for Rare’s recent Selena Gomez x Demi Lovato campaign. It also means rethinking the send-out itself. Booker’s test is whether it’s worth filming. She also works as a model and content creator, so experiences it from the receiving end too. “I get a million boxes a day, and I barely post any of them. But I post the one I feel most compelled to take a photo or video of,” she says. This includes practical gifts: “Something I can use, like a fragrance tray,” or an experience. Luxury brands, she adds, often get it right by pairing a product with a way to use it, “like a skincare product with a gift of a facial.”

Given the diminishing impact of gifting, and the high cost of paid placements, some brands are leaning further into loaning for high-profile talent. “Each sample is worth thousands of dollars,” says Mitola, which is why premium labels like Colleen Allen lean on loans rather than gifts. “When we agree to dress somebody, in a way we’re paying for that moment, because we won’t be able to place it again in a big way once it’s worn.” The goal is consistency, to establish recognizability for the brand. “When you see a talent in Colleen’s work without a tag underneath it, you can just tell energetically that it is probably Colleen’s dress.”

When brands do carry out traditional gifting, they need to re-think the channels they go through. Chalmers has stopped gifting VIPs through their personal teams altogether. “We see a much faster return by working directly with stylists,” she says. Chalmers opens her Hollywood showroom on the weekends for last-minute fittings, since stylists rarely have time to wait for an international shipment. It pays off: when Sabrina Carpenter wore Australian label Kat The Label, the style immediately built a waitlist. Charli XCX’s wears landed just as press began covering the peek-through bra trend, placing Kat at the center of that conversation and boosting its global awareness almost overnight, says Chalmers.

Charli XCX performing at the 2026 Airbnb.org Gala in a peek-through bra look.

Michelle feels that stylist-placed pieces can translate better. “It has intention behind it. It’s chosen for them, fitted to them, and part of a bigger story. It means something.”

Sometimes, the best placement isn’t a placement at all. Jennifer Lawrence first came to Colleen Allen through being dressed in the brand by her stylist, Ryan Hastings, and soon became a fan. Recently, she was photographed in the label’s chartreuse velvet house coat, which she’d bought herself, and it sold out immediately. The moment that landed was the one no amount of brand investment could have teed up.

It’s why the stylist relationship is worth nurturing. “A PR I trust will lead you to a new like-minded brand that wasn’t on your radar,” says Michelle. “I go back to brands that I connect with, that fit the body well, that use great fabrics, that have great PR teams that make moments happen.”

#6688. Hidden in the Viral Last Ditch Debacle: How to Keep Lesbian Bars Alive

By September of this year, Jackie Matellian had spent months living in her truck while working several jobs to keep Last Ditch, a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, open. She was the last remaining original founder, and the bar was in deep financial trouble. According to reporting by The Boston Globe, workers had gone unpaid, Matellian was carrying a $50,000 start-up loan, and the landlord wanted $3,900 in overdue rent.

Last Ditch had been built to do things most bars don’t even attempt. It welcomed lesbians, transsexuals, and other queer people who couldn’t afford the cover, offered a free store with food, clothing and harm-reduction supplies, and required KN95 masks or better. For immunocompromised patrons, those precautions made it possible to have a night out without gambling with their health. The bar’s radical inclusiveness was part of why people cared about it—and part of what its owners were struggling to finance it.

Desperate for cash, the bar’s management announced a policy shift with a cheery Instagram post: Saturday nights would become mask-optional. The gamble backfired. By treating accessibility as negotiable, the bar alienated immunocompromised regulars without attracting enough new customers to pay the rent. Follow-up stumbles culminated in a marathon three-and-a-half-hour community meeting that collapsed without a resolution. Rather than saving the venue, the policy pivot left Last Ditch with the worst of both worlds: fractured community trust and an unresolved financial crisis.

The drama became national entertainment, right up until October 26, when Last Ditch announced its soft closure.

The spectators moved on, but one issue remains: expecting one struggling lesbian bar to compensate for the failures of an entire social infrastructure is absurd. The irony is that Western Massachusetts built the blueprint for combating exactly this.

Women in the area have been finding ways to share the costs of lesbian social life for decades. UMass Amherst documents more than 400 lesbian and feminist groups active in the region between 1968 and 1978. Northampton had the Common Womon Club, Lesbian Gardens, Womonfyre Books, and the Nutcracker’s Suite self-defense dojo. These were places women built to make their social lives and organizing possible outside institutions that routinely excluded them.

In 1976, the women behind Common Womon pooled money to buy property through Ceres Inc., the nonprofit they’d formed, then financed renovations with help from donations and a loan. The adjacent storefront provided rental income and housed the Nutcracker’s Suite, then Womonfyre Books, so control of the property also gave the women a way to make room for other projects and help pay for the place they shared. Common Womon also collected sliding-scale membership dues, while the Valley Women’s History Collaborative lists benefits for the Common Womon Club that helped keep it going.

The womon-spelling and the names are fun to inherit; I also want us to inherit the ability to put actual premises under our control. For Last Ditch, that begins with finding out whether a new set of owners can remain in the building on terms the business can afford.

Matellian had already told the Globe she planned to turn the bar into a cooperative. For that to relieve the pressure on her, new members would need to take responsibility for work she’d been doing and agree on how the existing debt would be handled. But calling it a cooperative wouldn’t do much for Matellian if she was still the person everyone called whenever something went wrong. Sharing authority has to include sharing responsibility for the work, with limits on what any one person is expected to carry.

Sharing ownership would give people more power over decisions and occasions to disagree about them. Common Womon closed in 1982, while Womonfyre lasted until 1989. Womonfyre faced harassment and threats from outside the lesbian community as well as conflicts over sexual politics and what the shop should sell. Its archive preserves those disputes alongside bank statements and instructions for running the store.

A cooperative at Last Ditch would need procedures for making decisions in tandem with conflict resolution. Which is why I like that the Womonfyre archive makes room for instructions on running the shop alongside political disputes. A disagreement over how to run a bar doesn’t become abuse because people are arguing. Treating every conflict as a verdict on someone’s character makes it harder to agree on a change, because the argument can continue long after the conduct has stopped or the policy has been reversed.

Making that possible at Last Ditch requires paid training and a written account of all this work. A cooperative whose members can debate the mission for four hours but can’t cover a shift or pay its debt will end up crushing the same woman behind the bar.

If Last Ditch is to survive, its next incarnation must trade endless character trials for operational infrastructure: shared labor, transparent books, and creative financing strategies.

If one thing the Globe’s reporting revealed, it is that one commercial bar bearing the weight of an entire community’s social safety crushes everyone under impossible expectations. Instead, we must look for ways to anchor the politics in practical economics, share the burden, and build a room strong enough to hold the argument without tearing down the house.

Anyone asking the community to save Last Ditch needs to be prepared to share control of what survives.

#6686. Remember When James Bond Was an Adidas Guy?

The search for the next James Bond continues. Over the weekend, Deadline reported that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had also screen-tested for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor. But once we've worked out who's getting the tux, there's another question: What sneakers is he going to wear?

As it turns out, their predecessor Daniel Craig got that bit right, too. In 2012's Skyfall, 007 turns up for his MI6 fitness tests in a navy SIS tracksuit and Adidas Gazelle IIs. In the scene, Bond's trying to prove he's fit enough to get back to work, and it's not going particularly well. As a viewer, you'd be forgiven for missing the shoes.

Daniel Craig as James Bond in Skyfall (2012).

But take another look. These were off-the-shelf Gazelles from Adidas's spring 2011 line, the sort that anyone could have picked up the year before the film came out. Bond is a guy whose wardrobe gets examined down to the last cufflink, and there he was in a regular pair of Adidas. His pair came in “dark indigo” suede with “Argentina blue” stripes, white rubber soles, and gold Gazelle lettering along the sides.

(There's a slight difference between the shoes a civilian could buy and the ones in the movie, though. The retail pair had a light blue heel tab, while Bond's appears darker. The fan website Bond Lifestyle suggests the costume department may have changed it, although that hasn't been officially confirmed.)

The Gazelle launched in 1966 as a multipurpose training shoe, and was the German sportswear giant's first-ever sneaker made from suede. The choice to put Bond in the shoe felt notable in more ways than one: In the training scene, the slim sole kept things nice and light underfoot, and the color combo went perfectly with his trackies. But there's also the Gazelle's place in British culture, from the football terraces in the ’80s to the Britpop crowd in the ’90s. So, it makes sense for a Gen-X British spy.

By 2021, Adidas had an official collab to go with No Time to Die. The collection featured all Ultraboost running shoes, with slight nods to Bond's tuxedos and Safin's porcelain mask. The “Q Branch” edition even had a hidden compartment in the lacing cage, handy if your gym shorts don't have pockets.

For a pair that came from a regular ol' Adidas collection, Bond's OG Gazelles are surprisingly difficult to find now. But if you fancy something similar without spending the next six months refreshing eBay, you can start with these.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.
