#6685. At Shanghai’s International Import Festival, Global Brands Rethink China’s Role

As the global luxury industry searches for its next growth engine, some of its biggest players have doubled down on China in recent years. Their ambition was clear at the China International Import Expo (CIIE), a flagship government-backed trade event in Shanghai that has become a key stage for global brands to signal their value in the world’s second largest economy.

On November 5, the ninth CIIE opened in Shanghai, drawing a record 4,100-plus overseas exhibitors across the five-day event. From luxury conglomerates LVMH, Kering and Richemont, to sportswear giants like Nike, and beauty powerhouses like L’Oréal, this time, brands arrived with more than new products to unveil.

Dolce & Gabbana Beauty showcased fragrances, makeup and interactive AI experiences.

But this year’s CIIE tells a bigger story than another wave of international brands courting Chinese consumers. While many Western players have bet heavily on China’s recovery, the luxury market remains under pressure. According to Bain & Co., Mainland China luxury sales fell 3-5% in 2025, following a much steeper 17-19% contraction in 2024. Despite early signs of recovery, the latest earnings suggest a fragile rebound. LVMH reported a 5% organic decline in its fashion and leather goods division in the third quarter of 2026, citing softer conditions in China, while Kering flagged weaker store traffic in Mainland China as a drag on Gucci’s performance. Increasingly, Chinese shoppers are scrutinizing prices, questioning brand value, and increasingly prioritizing experiences over possessions.

Against this backdrop, a more consequential shift is taking shape. China is no longer simply a market where global brands compete for growth. It is increasingly a space for testing ideas, forging partnerships and shaping strategies that could influence their future far beyond the nation.

At this year’s CIIE, the industry’s biggest names are placing different bets on what comes next — and what role China will play in getting them there.

“If you want to understand China, you have to come to CIIE,” Marc-Antoine Jamet, secretary general of LVMH, tells Vogue Business, explaining why the French luxury conglomerate continues to participate in the annual event. “The CIIE is a window on Chinese society, a window on the Chinese economy, a window on Chinese policy,” he says. But its value extends beyond simply observing the market. “If you want to meet your suppliers, if you want to meet your partners, if you want to meet local authorities [...] that’s a place where you can start a dialogue with the whole China.”

This year, LVMH brought seven of its maisons and businesses to Shanghai: Louis Vuitton, Dior, Bulgari, Tiffany & Co., Guerlain, Hennessy, and Sephora. Rather than focusing exclusively on product launches, the group used the occasion to explore the historical and cultural connections between its brands and China.

Louis Vuitton, for example, traced its longstanding ties with the country through the art of travel. A recreation of the maison’s historic Asnières salon featured three heritage trunks, including a studded leather trunk crafted by a Cantonese trunk maker in the 19th century. By placing an object of Chinese craftsmanship within its own heritage narrative, Louis Vuitton offered a reminder that the relationship between European luxury and China extends well beyond the country’s emergence as a major consumer market. This is wise in a moment when Chinese consumers are increasingly seeking authentic cultural connections, rather than familiar Chinese motifs repackaged by Western luxury brands.

Dior, meanwhile, drew a line from its iconic 1947 Bar suit to current creative director Jonathan Anderson’s contemporary reinterpretations of the house’s signature silhouette, bringing together fashion history, craftsmanship, and creative reinvention.

A bar jacket look from Jonathan Anderson’s Dior FW26 Couture at the expo.

Kering is taking the conversation a step further, positioning Chinese creativity as part of its future strategy. Returning to CIIE for the eighth consecutive year, the French luxury group presented an exhibition inspired by its strategic vision — True Luxury, Next Luxury — with Chinese contemporary art at its center.

The pavilion’s exterior featured an experimental calligraphic interpretation of the Thousand Character Classic, a traditional Chinese text dating back more than a thousand years, by artist Wang Dongling. In the courtyard, artist Ren Tianjin’s Taihu Stone: East Wind brought together calligraphy and sculpture, drawing on the aesthetics of traditional Chinese scholar’s rocks through a contemporary lens.

The Kering pavilion featured an experimental calligraphic exterior and Ren Tianjin's Taihu Stone in the courtyard.

“For Kering, China is not only one of our most important markets, it’s a vital force of innovation and creative inspiration,” said Jean-Marc Duplaix, Kering’s COO and CEO of Kering Jewelry, at CIIE. “Guided by this vision, we’re executing our global innovation and talent strategy in China.”

That thinking is beginning to translate into product strategy. On November 6, Qeelin, the Chinese-rooted fine jewelry house owned by Kering, unveiled Qeelin Gold, a new gold jewelry brand, alongside its debut collection, Bajing.

The launch marks a notable departure from the localization playbook traditionally favored by international luxury groups, which has often centered on limited-edition products, festive campaigns, and market-specific retail experiences.

Instead, Kering is looking to build on a distinctly Chinese cultural and commercial opportunity. Gold has deep cultural significance in China, where it has long been associated with prosperity, celebration and the preservation of wealth. As consumers increasingly seek jewelry that combines intrinsic material value with contemporary design, Qeelin Gold represents an attempt to translate that heritage into a new luxury proposition.

Qeelin Gold was unveiled at the Kering pavillion.

China’s booming domestic gold jewelry sector offers further incentive. The meteoric rise of Laopu Gold, alongside Kering Ventures’s investment in Chinese jeweler Borland, underscores the growing appeal of homegrown luxury brands — and the opportunity for international groups to capitalize on this momentum.

Richemont, meanwhile, approached the conversation through craftsmanship and heritage. The Swiss luxury group brought Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Vacheron Constantin, Alaïa, and Montblanc to the expo. Among the highlights were Vacheron Constantin’s Year of the Goat timepiece from its Chinese zodiac collection, a Cartier high jewelry creation interpreting the maison’s signature panther through intricate construction, and a Montblanc special-edition writing instrument paying tribute to martial arts icon Bruce Lee.

Cartier showcased an interpretation of its signature panther whereas Montblac took inspiration from martial arts icon Bruce Lee.

Sportswear giants are taking a more direct approach at CIIE, putting Chinese consumers at the center of product development and innovation.

At Adidas’s expanded 500-square-meter pavilion, a globally debuted collection of Chinese-inspired jackets sat alongside performance running technology and professional sports equipment. According to Adidas, more than 65% of the products it sells in China are now designed by local teams, while 95% are manufactured domestically. The brand even staged a runway show in Shanghai last year, to showcase the brand’s local work. More significantly, around a quarter of the products developed by its Chinese design teams have made their way into the brand’s global distribution network. One example is the Chinese-inspired jacket first showcased at last year’s CIIE. When launched in North America, 12,000 units sold out in just 27 minutes, according to the company.

The Adidas pavilion featured Chinese-inspired jackets, performance running technology and professional sports equipment.

Nike, meanwhile, is placing greater emphasis on localizing the innovation process itself. Returning to CIIE for the seventh consecutive year, the American sportswear giant showcased its Radical AirFlow apparel cooling technology, alongside new basketball and performance running footwear, as well as locally developed collections including Nike Swooshfly, designed with Chinese younger consumers in mind.

Speaking to Vogue Business, Flavia Cervantes, VP of local product creation for Nike Greater China, explained the thinking behind the company’s expanding creative operations in the country. Rather than relying solely on conventional market research, the team is immersing itself in the lives of young Chinese consumers — from trail running and hiking to community gatherings and music festivals — to better understand how they move, dress, and express themselves. These observations, she explained, feed directly into decisions around materials, silhouettes and product innovation. “Having a local team in China allows us to drive innovation and product development at the pace of young Chinese consumers,” she said.

Nike exhibited locally developed collections such as the Nike Swooshfly

Arc’teryx, making its CIIE debut, brought another dimension of product innovation into focus: what happens to performance gear after it is sold. The outdoors specialist showcased its Sperro SV technical shell jacket, the first product developed under System 0, its circular innovation platform. Beyond waterproofing, wind protection and breathability, the jacket has been designed with maintenance, repair and eventual material recovery in mind. It also features a digital product passport (DPP), allowing consumers to scan a QR code for information on product care and repair services.

Arc’teryx showcased its Sperro SV technical shell jacket and ReBird services, emphasizing product care and repair.

Beyond luxury and sportswear, another theme emerged at this year’s CIIE is that international brands are increasingly competing for a place in Chinese consumers’ lifestyles, not just their closets.

Making its CIIE debut, Ralph Lauren presented four immersive spaces inspired by the American West, coastal living, country estates and urban sophistication. Spanning fashion, homeware and hospitality, the exhibition reflected the brand’s longstanding strategy of selling an aspirational way of life.

Fellow newcomers Woolrich and Bogner introduced further options in premium outdoors and lifestyle categories, while established players focused on deepening consumer engagement.

Beauty groups are pursuing a similar strategy, increasingly combining product innovation with technology and personalized experiences.

L’Oréal Group, returning for its ninth consecutive year, expanded its presence to 28 brands, introducing names including Color Wow and Skinbetter Science alongside AI-powered beauty technology. Estée Lauder Companies showcased 17 brands and more than 80 new products, including a Mac Cosmetics setting product developed with Asian skin tones in mind. Dolce & Gabbana Beauty, meanwhile, used the expo to highlight its expanding China ambitions through fragrances, makeup and interactive AI experiences.

Nine editions in, CIIE offers a revealing snapshot of how international brands are rethinking the fast-changing market. For years, international brands came to China in search of growth. Increasingly, they are also looking to China for ideas on where growth might come from next.

#6684. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6682. 70 Best Gifts for Women in 2026, According to GQ

When it comes to buying gifts for the women in your life, we have one rule: Shop from her wishlist, not her to-do list. Maybe she's got a Sephora's worth of serums in her bathroom, a small fortune invested in vintage Italian glassware, or a closet full of capital-F fashion with “nothing to wear.” Whatever her particular brand of enthusiasm, we've got it well covered, from the latest and greatest beauty to old-fashioned fineries in cashmere and silk. Below, an assortment of some of the best gifts for women at every price point.

Good gifts don't stop here. Explore all our gift guides, then sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more excellent ideas.

British knitwear label &Daughter can count us among its devoted followers, not least for its Sligo V-neck, a Scottish lambswool sweater with a slightly shrunken fit that makes the traditional style feel decidedly of the moment.

Collina Strada made its name from its playful, offbeat designs, and this ring is the easiest way for her to add a little “festive” flair this season without resorting to sequins, though sequins are also welcome.

There's been a lot of commotion around the larger version of Coach's Kisslock bag, but this smaller iteration is every bit as chic. With its structured shape and classic clasp, it's prim and proper in a good way.

This Fair Isle scrunchie from Banana is a cheery finishing touch that makes even the simplest ponytail feel festive. If the wintry knit pattern ain't her thing, there are a few other fun designs to choose from.

We love a precious itsy-bitsy watch, and so does Brynn Wallner, the watch writer behind Dimepiece, who teamed up with Timex to offer up this dainty little number. It's simple, does the job, and makes a lovely gift for someone who feels the same way.

Alexa Chung has a few different irons in the fire these days, but perhaps none hotter than these snakeskin mules with a cute block heel.

A little playful, and straight to the point. Emily Dawn Long's IYKYK wares are modern classics at this point, and an easy gift for those you know who do indeed know.

A rugby for the girls. Boxy and cropped, this one from Buck Mason might finally get her to stop borrowing yours.

Sophie Buhai's signature egg pendant has been around since she first started, and a decade later, I gotta say, it's still a very good egg.

Done up in crocodile-embossed leather, Saint Laurent's giant bowling bag is a canny investment for someone who wants one very good bag to do it all: an everyday carryall during the week, and a posh getaway bag for the next weekender.

A mainstay from New York-based label Silphium, this leather sling bag flaunts a sculptural teardrop shape and an adjustable knotted strap. Each one is made to order, so you better get to it.

No one, at least that I know of, has ever been disappointed by a pair of Comme Si boxers, which can and absolutely should be worn out of the house.

A double-breasted peacoat is good. A double-breasted peacoat cut with these proportions is even better. Ideal for tossing over just about anything.

If she's a self-proclaimed cold girl, Quince's fuzzy merino wool balaclava will keep her noggin (and ears and neck) nice and toasty.

Earlier this year, Acne Studios followed up its much-loved collaboration with perfumer Frédéric Malle with a body wash scented with peach, sandalwood, and musk.

Pepper and rose make a glorious pairing, especially in the hands of Dries Van Noten, who makes some of the best formulations in the business.

Summer Fridays has bundled up a few sunny-day essentials—its lip butter balm, mineral milk sunscreen, and vanilla eau de parfum—in a charming little mini tote perfect for bringing poolside.

We recommended Therabody's Depuffing Wand last year, and we're running it back because it's just so dang good at what it does. Hot and cold treatments in one wonderfully unfussy little device make it a welcome addition to her skincare routine.

Combining gua sha with red-light therapy was only a matter of time. Ora Method's LED gua sha tool also throws gentle vibration into the mix, so she gets a little massaging, depuffing, and skin rejuvenation all in one go.

Chanel No. 5 needs no introduction, but I'll give it one anyway. Rose, jasmine, and a little citrus make up this grand dame of fragrances, which smells just as good today as it did a century ago.

I won't pretend to know the first thing about hair tools, but the women I consulted for this guide assure me that Shark's FlexStyle is a worthy alternative to the considerably pricier Dyson Airwrap. Defer to their expertise and pocket the difference.

A good hair day is a gift. Kérastase's holiday duo helps make them happen. Inside: the brand's cult-favorite Elixir Ultime hair oil for shine, plus its night serum to work some overnight magic.

The original Glossier You fragrance is a modern classic, and this gift set doubles down on it, with a full-size bottle for her dresser and a travel-size one to take wherever she goes.

A little color for her lips, a little flush for her cheeks, all in one. Pleasing's Big Lip + Cheek is a clever twofer from Harry Styles' beauty brand, which she'll be impressed you know about in the first place.

Look at the lapels on this thing! Hommey's striped robe makes lounging around the house feel like a grand affair, and it comes in all sorts of lively, unexpected colorways.

She can wear these slippers from Mallorca-based Camper while padding around the house, but they'll look just as good out and about. And with a cushy EVA footbed and rubber outsoles, she can be comfortably be out and about for hours.

You can't walk down the street these days without spotting someone clutching an iced matcha, and those daily cafe runs add up. Fellow's beautifully made set, launched last year, can help them save some green while getting their fix.

I'm a coffee drinker through and through, but I'd consider switching allegiances to tea if it meant getting to use this teapot from Balmuda. Just looking at the thing feels therapeutic.

This modish Herman Miller throw features an archival design by Alexander Girard, primary-color enthusiast and founding director of the company's textile division, brought to life by the good folks at Pendleton.

Loewe just added a Pistachio scent to its delicious range of candles. Good luck resisting the urge to light it every night.

No matter how she likes her martinis, they'll always be a little dirty in Maison Balzac's glasses, thanks to the playful glass olives nestled inside. The set comes with two glasses and a matching olive plate.

Rocco's game-changing beverage fridge now has a more affordable sibling. The Essential holds more than 100 cans and costs considerably less than the flagship Super Smart Fridge, while retaining the same compressor.

If status gardenwear is a category she's invested in, there's no bigger flex than a Haws watering can. In cherry red, it feels like a little luxury for reviving your house plants.

With all the high-tech sunrise clocks on the market these days, we've managed to overcomplicate the alarm clock. Maybe some things don't need reinventing. Take this handsome one from Arne Jacobsen, the Danish design legend who also gave us the egg chair.

Fresh on the scene, Typical had the sorta boring idea to rethink the bath towel by adding 2% spandex, making it stretchy enough to move with you and stay securely wrapped. Turns out boring ideas can be pretty great, and these towels are a real treat.

Dorai's sleek stone sink caddy is made from diatomaceous earth, a freakishly absorbent material that wicks away water in seconds, keeping things from sitting in a soggy mess.

For their second collaboration, Sandy Liang and Baggu brought back the much-loved print, this time in an especially good shade of blue.

If they have a passion for water and a good water bottle, Kinto’s is worth a look. Made from recycled materials with the transparency of glass, it’s just a nice thing to carry around all day.

Nothing released a gaggle of great listening gear this year, and the Headphone (a) is a standout. Cheaper than the flagship Headphone (1), it still delivers superb sound, an absurd 135 hours of battery life, and some excellent color options. One of the best pairs we tested all year at this price.

Bose has finally made its first wired noise-canceling earbuds. Expect them to be a hot commodity among the wired-headphone evangelists, who can now tune out the world without compromising their principles.

Apple's new entry-level laptop might be marketed to students, but it's also a very good laptop for anyone who just needs to do regular laptop things. Browsing, emailing, streaming, the occasional spreadsheet—the Neo handles the everyday stuff without demanding a small fortune for the privilege of owning a fruit-embossed gadget.

Apple's new AirPods 5 come in two tiers, and the more giftable of the two is the version with the wireless charging case. You get longer battery life and swipe-to-adjust volume controls right on the stems.

Apple's flagship ticker takes care of the everyday stuff, from keeping tabs on workouts and sleep to saving you from fishing your phone out of your pocket every five minutes. There's also a new chip built to handle a smarter, AI-powered Siri, which should make the world's most popular smart watch that much more useful.

Ray-Ban Meta's Burbank glasses are all about audio: music, podcasts, and calls, without sticking anything in your ears. And, to be absolutely clear, there's no camera. None.

Alex Mill's leather phone lanyard, made by leather goods experts at Billykirk, keeps their phone close at hand and looks pretty good doing it.

You may spotted a Bailey Hikawa phone case out in the wild. They're pretty hard to miss. With bold, undulating shapes and eye-catching colors, they also double as a stand, propping your phone up vertically or horizontally.

Cotopaxi and Fujifilm teamed up for this handy setup. Inside: an Instax Mini 13 instant camera, a shoulder bag and camera strap done up in Cotopaxi's signature riot of color, and film to get them snapping right out of the box.

Taking its cues from Kodak's '70s-era 110 camera, Camp Snap offers a screen-free digital experience with an 8MP sensor, which is modest by today's standards, but entirely the point.

You know Brick, but have you met Brick Night? The new bedside gadget uses Bluetooth to automatically block distracting apps when you enter the bedroom during, putting an end to late-night doomscrolling without a second thought.

Toronto-based jewelry designer Steff Eleoff makes brilliantly designed sculptural covers that slip over an Oura (or “tech”) ring, turning a piece of werable tech into something they'll actually want to show off.

U-Turn's Orbit Plus is one of the finest midrange turntables around. This version has a built-in phono preamp, so she can get straight to spinning records with a pair of powered speakers.

Nothing’s sub-brand CMF has made its first portable Bluetooth speaker, a peculiar little contraption that bears an uncanny resemblance to a milk carton. Which, in a sea of anonymous black cylinders, is the point.

Twelve South's Valet gives her phone a proper place to recharge, with a handy catchall for keys, jewelry, and whatever else tends to accumulate around the house.

No one expects much from a charger in the design department, but when someone actually tries, it can make all the difference. Counterpart's looks great plugged into the wall, and its retractable cord is a genuine pleasure to use.

Whoop's new Meridian band is a welcome reminder of where fitness trackers are headed: they no longer need to look like fitness trackers. An elegant little upgrade for anyone who wants to keep tabs on their health without advertising the fact.

Part sweatpant, part track pant, this oversized pair from lululemon has a satisfyingly weighty feel and the kind of relaxed fit she'll wanna live in.

Between their office, hotel rooms, and Airbnbs, there's a lot of bone-dry air out there. Canopy's new portable humidifier makes it easy to add a little moisture wherever they go, with a dose of aromatherapy to boot.

These comfy silicone earplugs dial down the volume on everyday distractions, whether she's trying to focus at work or enjoy a little peace and quiet at home. And unlike those disposable foam plugs, they're actually nice to look at.

How could Theragun possibly improve on its already excellent mini massage gun, you ask? By adding heat, of course. The Mini Plus combines percussive massage with warming therapy to help loosen up sore muscles.

Again, never underestimate the restorative powers of a little targeted heat. Or, in this case, heat from head to toe. HigherDose's sauna blanket is easy to set up and use, and delivers one hell of a sweat session without requiring a trip to an actual hot box.

Some nervous systems could use a little extra TLC. An Ori's First Breath aromatherapy inhaler is turned from solid wood and filled with soothing botanicals.

This set from Kate McLeod of solid bath and shower oils puts cocoa butter and jojoba oil to work, delivering a generous dose of plant-based moisture without another bottle cluttering the tub.

She's already made one great choice. Don't make her question it.

#6681. The Mysterious Fridge Hacks Hitting Grocery Stores

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the Cheesecake Factory culture war.

Death, taxes, and Martha Stewart doing something weird online every six to eight weeks: These are the constants in our ever-chaotic lives. This round involved a quickly deleted Instagram post showing Stewart apparently dressed as a homeless person—she was holding a clipboard (?) with a message in marker that read “I am hungry help me!!”

She released a series of statements apologizing for the gaffe, and at one point seemed to blame Today show host Craig Melvin, who, she said, spilled chocolate on the sweater she’d planned on wearing to a costume party later that night, forcing her to improvise a new costume on the fly.

But enough of Martha! We have more important things to worry about.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the mysterious refrigeration system hacks plaguing Europe, DC's newly minted foie gras ban, the GLP-1 gap relationship, and a democratic victory is celebrated at a Whataburger, naturally.

Dozens of supermarkets across seven countries were the victims of hacking that took control of their refrigeration systems this week. The hackers shifted grocery freezers into defrost mode, the freezers began blowing hot air onto the frozen food, and, in some, temperatures rose to 122 degrees. Needless to say a lot of food was deemed spoiled and had to be thrown out.

Three weeks ago, similar attacks hit grocery stores in France. It was the same story: defrost mode, hot air, lots of wasted food and money. Officials are investigating who may be responsible, but so far the culprits and their motives remain a mystery. The BBC reports that experts believe hackers in Russia or Iran—or simply teenagers playing a prank—could be responsible.

Could something like this happen in the US? Well, it sort of already has. In August six military bases across the country reported some odd refrigeration malfunctions—the same kind we’ve been seeing in Europe. The Pentagon is investigating the incident as a suspected hack, but that’s about as much information as we can glean.

The FBI on Thursday issued a warning about “malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world.”

As Democrats celebrated a resounding wave of victories in this week’s midterm elections, so too did duck and goose lovers. Washington, DC, voted to approve a ballot measure banning the sale and production of foie gras. It was a controversial issue in the area, as I covered in last week’s Open Tab video, which saw big name chefs come forward to defend the making, selling, and eating of foie gras. The discourse got heated, topical Halloween costumes abounded.

The ban will go into effect July 1, 2027, so foie-heads have some time to get their fill. But it’s not that simple. A New York foie gras company has said it will take legal action against the ban, calling it “unconstitutional on several grounds." To put the ban in effect would face further logistical barriers too. DC’s chief financial officer has estimated it would cost more than $300,000 over four fiscal years to implement it—money that’s not currently allocated in the budget.

Despite the upcoming ban, Bart Hutchins, chef and co-owner of Butterworth’s who was one of the ban’s most vocal opponents, has said he’ll continue serving foie gras in his restaurants. “I will still be serving it for another decade,” he told the Washington Post.

What happens when one partner gets on a GLP-1 and the other partner doesn’t? We know that GLP-1’s can shift your sex drive, and that they can have an effect on your mental health, but often, it seems, there’s anecdotal evidence that they can have a profound effect on your relationships. A report in the Washington Post details how, for some couples, starting a GLP-1 can disrupt a couple's routines and equilibrium—deciding on a date night restaurant, for instance—which can create divisions. There simply isn’t enough data to measure how GLP-1’s might be linked to divorce rates, but some experts point to statistics attached to bariatric surgeries, another weight loss intervention, which found that married couples are twice as likely to get divorced after getting the procedure.

Midterm elections in the US brought a number of historic firsts, including the first Muslim senator (Michigan), the first openly gay man senator (New Hampshire), and the first Black woman governor (Georgia). Notably, voters managed to flip Texas, turning the state blue for the first time in decades.

How did Texas Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa celebrate their wins? At a Whataburger. It’s a surprisingly poignant statement about the affordability politics that was foundational to many Democratic wins this election cycle. Read on to learn more.

#6680. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6679. Culture Watch: What to See and Where to Go in November

Culture Watch is a series spotlighting the intersection of fashion and art, bringing you the latest must-see exhibitions, pop-ups, installations, and more.

November is a good month to make a little room in your calendar. As the holiday season starts to gather pace, galleries, brands, and creative spaces are offering plenty of reasons to get out and look around. In New York, Salon Art + Design returns for its 15th year, while Loro Piana presents its “Master of Cashmere” installation at The Brant Foundation; farther afield, international exhibitions offer even more to explore. Check out all of this month’s best cultural happenings below.

Loro Piana Names Its Cashmere of the Year and Unveils a ‘Master of Cashmere’ Installation

Loro Piana put cashmere in the spotlight at The Brant Foundation in New York, where it marked the 11th edition of its Cashmere of the Year Award. Established in 2015 and held stateside for the first time, the prize recognizes the herders who produce the finest cashmere fiber. Coinciding with the honor, which went to three couples of cashmere herders from Inner Mongolia, is “Master of Cashmere: The Quest for Fiber Excellence,” an installation that traces the material from its origins to the Maison’s work with it. The multi-room experience features archival sketches, explanatory timelines, and, of course, soft-to-the-touch cashmere.

Taylor Swift, take note: famously hard-to-get-into New York City hotspot The Corner Store has officially landed at The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, marking its first-ever location outside Manhattan. Expect its adventurous martinis, signature wood-paneled interiors by Rockwell Group, and a handful of Vegas-exclusive menu additions, including a Butcher’s Counter serving up wagyu tomahawk and porterhouse steaks.

Salon Art + Design Returns to the Park Avenue Armory for Its 15th Year

The 15th edition of Salon Art + Design is now on view at the Park Avenue Armory—and it’s one of its most immersive, expansive editions yet. As is tradition, the event brings together collectible design, fine art, and jewelry. The event is open through November 8. Standouts include Jean Dunand’s 1929 La Forêt lacquered screen, Michel Dufet’s 1918 daybeds, and Jean Royère’s illuminated desk. Fernando Mastrangelo’s totem lamps add a sculptural note, while the jewelry lineup includes pieces from Fernando Jorge, Mellerio, Cora Sheibani, and Viltier.

Lara Saget Debuts Her First New York Solo Show, ‘And the World Came Apart’

Lara Saget brings more than a decade of material experimentation to her first solo exhibition in New York. At Trotter&Sholer’s new Elizabeth Street space, her sculptures and wearable works fuse glass, stone, and metal through heat, pressure, and time. Drawing on geological processes and NASA data, the show moves from ancient natural formations to humanity’s rapid impact on the planet.

The Phillips Collection Opens ‘Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea’

Milton Avery went to Gloucester, Massachusetts, to “live like an artist,” then brought Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko along for summers of creative exchange. In Washington, D.C., The Phillips Collection’s “Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea” brings together watercolors and color-drenched canvases, tracing what those Cape Ann days set in motion.

Tate St Ives Spotlights Wilhelmina Barns-Graham

What does a landscape feel like in the body? Scottish artist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham spent eight decades exploring that question through art shaped by sensation and memory. The retrospective at Tate St Ives in Cornwall, England, is the most comprehensive survey of her work, moving from early landscapes and studio interiors to later works alive with bold color and sweeping gestures.

#6678. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Founded in 2023, Counsel Health is an AI-powered primary care platform that combines medical AI with a network of physicians to deliver personalized medical guidance and treatment. The company has agreed to be acquired by Finnish smart ring maker Oura for $625 million, as Oura looks to move beyond biometric tracking toward more holistic, tailored health insights and actionable medical care. The acquisition will integrate Counsel’s AI and on-demand physicians with Oura’s continuous health data collection, enabling users to access medical advice, prescriptions, lab result interpretations, and chronic care support through the Oura app.

Funding and round: Acquisition, $625 million.

Investor comments: “Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale. “Together, we can create a new model of care that extends the current healthcare paradigm by delivering an experience that’s more immediate, personalized, and proactive.”

Company description: Founded in 1889, Lee has made its marks as one of the biggest heritage names in denim. The American brand generates an average of $1.5 billion in annual sales across 73 countries, of which almost 40% comes from outside the US and Canada. New York-based Authentic Brands Group has successfully acquired Lee from Kontoor Brands in an effort to expand Lee into adjacent categories, including activewear and workwear, as well as lifestyle offerings.

Investor(s): Authentic Brands Group (portfolio includes: Guess, Juicy Couture, Reebok).

Investor comments: “We are thrilled to welcome Lee to the Authentic family,” said Jamie Salter, founder and executive chair of Authentic Brands Group. “Lee has the heritage, recognition and consumer loyalty we look for in a brand. By connecting Lee to Authentic’s global platform and the right partners in key markets, we see a significant opportunity to expand its reach through content, experiences and new product categories.”

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.

Company description: Scottish-born accessible luxury leather goods brand Strathberry has closed its second funding round, consisting of a growth investment from Soho Square Capital’s new Fund II, and marking the fund’s first investment. The funding comes on the heels of a strong year for Strathberry, which delivered 39% year-on-year growth in 2026 at $50.5 million. Soho Square’s investment will support Strathberry founders Guy and Leeanne Hundleby’s ambitions to accelerate the brand’s North America expansion.

Funding and round: Undisclosed minority investment valuing the company at approximately £100 million, second funding round.

Investor(s): Soho Square Capital’s Fund II.

Investor comments: “Strathberry is an exceptional brand with a rare combination of craftsmanship, a distinctive design signature and a genuinely international, loyal customer base. The label’s ‘high-end quality at accessible prices’ ethos is resonating with shoppers disillusioned with top luxury houses. Guy, Leeanne, and the team have created something special, and there is significant scope to grow the business internationally,” Soho Square Capital director David Steel said in a statement.

Company description: Thorne, the science-backed supplements brand founded in 1984, has entered into a definitive acquisition agreement with P&G. Thorne is currently owned by L Catterton’s Flagship Fund. It is now best known in the wellness space for its creatine product, leaning into the rise of the supplement and its various formats. The acquisition helps to further Thorne’s attempt at becoming the market’s most-trusted personalized health brand, as well as P&G’s aim to move its personal health business upmarket. The transaction is expected to close later this year, subject to regulatory approval.

Investor(s): Procter & Gamble (portfolio includes: Seven Seas, Oral-B, Pepto Bismol).

Investor comments: “Consumer interest in selfcare, prevention, wellness, and personalized health continues to grow, and Thorne strengthens our position in premium wellness with a trusted, science-backed brand that complements our existing portfolio,” CEO of P&G Health Care Paul Gama said.

Company description: Frasers Group has taken a 4.2% position in British luxury brand Burberry. Frasers, the company behind House of Fraser, Sports Direct and Flannels, is holding the position through put options, which gives Frasers Group the right to buy shares at a predetermined stock price. The company is also the second largest shareholder in Mulberry PLC.

Frasers Group has been on an investing spree of late, increasing its stake in Hugo Boss to 30.3% and offering a takeover proposal. Frasers Group also bought Matches for £52 million in December 2023, before it announced that it was going into administration; Matches was sold in December 2025 to form part of newly established luxury group Hulcan.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Solomei AI, the company behind the Callimacus platform, has announced that it has entered into an agreement for an investment from Salesforce. The investment will “support Callimacus’s efforts to expand its engineering and AI research capabilities, accelerate product development, and scale commercial operations across Europe and North America.” In January 2026, Callimacus, whose chairman is Brunello Cucinelli, was used to build the new e-commerce experience for the designer’s eponymous luxury brand.

Investor comments: “Brunello has always believed that technology should elevate humanity, and that conviction is at the heart of Callimacus,” said Marc Benioff, chair and CEO of Salesforce. “The team has developed an innovative platform that reimagines AI-powered experiences — bringing together conversational AI, enterprise context, and real-time personalization to create entirely new ways for businesses to engage with their customers.”

“Three years ago, Marc Benioff and I began an endeavor with mathematicians, philosophers, humanists, and technologists, from which Callimacus was born. Our idea was to create a simple, intuitive product capable of speaking the language of human beings; a sort of new web, without pages, categories, or predetermined paths, able to accompany the intent of each individual navigator. I look with great confidence and hope for the path that Callimacus will pursue with Salesforce’s investment,” Brunello Cucinelli, chairman of Solomei AI, added.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Merit is a US-based beauty brand designed as an antidote to using multiple, trend-led products — collapsing everyday cosmetics into a curated, minimal line-up. The investment is led by Vasiliki Petrou, managing partner at Semcap Beauty & Wellness, who also founded the Unilever Prestige division in 2014, spanning Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice, Hourglass, K18, and more.

Investor comments: “Merit is one of the most thoughtfully built brands in beauty, a true icon in the market. I love the timeless brand aesthetic, the simplified and edited approach to beauty, and the focus on the millennial and Gen X consumer, which is a significant white space in our industry. I am thrilled to support the continued global scaling of the brand,” Petrou said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28% (up from 26.06%), which demands an official takeover bid in line with German legislation. The move follows Frasers’s €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss believed was “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Frasers, now Hugo Boss’s largest shareholder, said its offer still stands through July 27.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: House of Fraser, Flannels, Sports Direct).

Company description: Syntetica is a French startup that transforms textile waste into recycled nylon through a proprietary chemical method that allows the processing of fabrics containing multiple materials. The funding will help Syntetica build its first commercial facility in France, which will be able to transform hundreds of tons of post-consumer textile waste annually. While Syntetica already works with labels such as Victoria’s Secret and Etam, it also plans to scale its recycling efforts and partner with more fashion brands.

Funding and round: $30 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Ecotechnologies 2 (portfolio includes: Standing Ovation, Mantle8), Lululemon (portfolio includes: Epoch Biodesign, Samsara Eco, Zymochem), MAS Holdings (portfolio includes: Victoria’s Secret, Calvin Klein, Gap), Swen Capital Partners, EQT Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal, Fleek is a wholesale vintage fashion marketplace. Fleek connects retailers and resellers with verified, secondhand clothing wholesalers worldwide, enabling them to source vintage inventory in bulk through a digital marketplace with integrated logistics and quality assurance.

Funding and round: $25 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Burda Principal Investments (portfolio includes: Vinted), Ebay Ventures, FJ Labs, H14, Andreessen Horowitz, HV Capital, Y Combinator, and more.

Company description: Whering is a digital wardrobe and styling app founded in 2020 by Bianca Rangecroft. The app enables users to catalogue the clothes they already own, create outfits, track wardrobe usage, and receive styling recommendations, with the aim of encouraging more intentional fashion consumption and reducing unnecessary purchases.

Investor(s): Ebay Ventures, Google AI Futures Fund.

Company description: Hair technology company Halo has developed its first product, HaloBraid. Launching in salons this fall, the device will be the first automated hair braiding tool that works alongside stylists to halve braiding time from as long as 10 hours per appointment. Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian’s VC firm Seven Seven Six is leading the investment into a business that was launched off the back of Yinka Ogunbiyi’s winning Harvard Innovation Labs pitch last year.

Investor(s): Seven Seven Six (portfolio includes: Anthropic, ElevenLabs, Flock Safety), Bling Capital (portfolio includes: Palantir, Gusto, Everlane), AlleyCorp (portfolio includes: ShopMy, Gilt Groupe, Business Insider).

Investor comments: “As an investor, I look for founders that see something broken that everyone else has accepted as fixed. Braiding is a perfect example: it is a process that has not materially changed in thousands of years, despite being one of the most popular hairstyles for millions of Americans and a significant part of the $270 billion salon services industry,” said Ohanian. “Yinka has introduced a novel technology to a traditionally manual and highly specialized professional service.”

Company description: L’Oréal Group has taken a stake in Indian personal care company Innovist. (Vogue Business reported on speculations back in March.) The company has a successful portfolio that includes Indian haircare brand Bare Anatomy, skincare brands Chemist at Play and Sunscoop, and bodycare brand Vinci Botanicals. The company was founded in 2018 by Rohit Chawla, Sifat Khurana, and Vimal Bhola with a focus on science-first formulations, transparent ingredients, and in-house research and development.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L’Oréal Group (portfolio includes: Cerave, La Roche-Posay, Vichy, Armani Beauty, SkinCeuticals).

Investor comments: “Our investment in this innovative Indian startup is a clear testament to our unwavering commitment to expanding L’Oréal’s footprint in India,” CEO Nicolas Hieronimus said. “By bringing together the very best of L’Oréal’s global expertise with Innovist’s high-performing, science-led products and deep-rooted understanding of the Indian consumer, I believe we are poised to shape the future of beauty in this dynamic market.”

Company description: Remedy is a dermatologist-developed skincare brand founded by Dr. Muneeb Shah in March 2024. The brand’s products target skin concerns such as dark spots, dryness, fine lines, dullness, keratosis pilaris, and sensitive skin. Remedy is stocked on Amazon, TikTok Shop and Target, the latter of which it partnered with in December 2025. The Series A investment will support the skincare brand with its next phase of growth, including advancing clinical research, expanding its product categories, and improving inventory. Remedy also plans to strengthen its formulation, testing, and consumer education.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): L Catterton (portfolio includes: Merit Beauty, Tula, Kopari, Elemis, Nutrafol, Intercos, Ex Nihilo).

Investor comments: “We seek to partner with exceptional founders building brands that will redefine categories, and we believe Remedy is uniquely modernizing dermatological skincare,” L Catterton partner Tehmina Haider said. “As both a clinician and a consumer educator, Dr. Shah has built a portfolio of simple, effective, and accessibly priced products that leverage advanced ingredient technologies to address real patient needs — and that is what will define the next generation of dermocosmetics. The brand’s rapid growth reflects deep consumer demand for affordable, clinically-grounded skincare, and we are thrilled to partner with the Remedy team on its next chapter.”

Company description: Bacchus is a London-based PR agency founded in 1998 by Anouschka Menzies and Charlotte Lurot, who currently lead the business alongside co-CEO Daize Washbourn. The agency specializes in luxury hospitality and culture, as well as in the prestige VIC and high-net-worth communities. With around 100 employees across seven offices (London, New York, Miami, LA, Dubai, Riyadh, and Doha), Bacchus generates annual sales of approximately $17 million. Its client portfolio includes Red Sea Global Residences, Six Senses, Auberge Resorts, the Victoria & Albert Museum, and Monte-Carlo Société des Bains de Mer.

Funding and round: Acquisition, majority stake.

Investor(s): Mazarine Group (portfolio includes: La Mode en Images, the show producer of Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Gucci).

Investor comments: “There were several objectives [with this investment],” Mazarine founder Paul-Emmanuel Reiffers tells Vogue Business. “First, we needed to add a public relations and influence branch to our group. Second, it had to be large enough for us to develop and accelerate it. With Bacchus, we’re starting from a platform that’s already large enough to consolidate operations, grow further, and open an office in Paris in the short to medium-term. Third, the acquisition gives us seven offices at once, providing an established global network and strengthening our geographic footprint. We already had a presence in Dubai, but now we’re able to establish ourselves in Riyadh, which is important because the Middle East is about to rebound strongly. We’re also strengthening our position in the US by expanding our network from New York to LA and Miami, allowing us to serve clients more effectively.”

He continues: “Finally, the acquisition aligns with what we see as the luxury sectors of tomorrow: hospitality, real estate, and longevity. As luxury brands increasingly move into these areas, we are positioning ourselves to support their expansion. It also creates valuable synergies, allowing us to integrate Bacchus’s expertise and network of personalities, influencers, and guests into our events.”

Company description: Bella Hadid has been slowly growing her fragrance brand Orebella since its launch in 2024. Now, with Series A funding from Silas Capital, which has previously invested in beauty brands including Makeup by Mario, Oak Essentials and Ilia, she can scale the line further across categories and markets.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Silas Capital (portfolio includes: Makeup by Mario, YSE Beauty, Dôen).

Company description: NYC-based startup Vetir is pitching itself as an AI luxury shopping app that goes beyond discovery and transactions to act as “a system of record for the wardrobe” for high-value consumers. In practice, this is something of an AI stylist that learns from the data users share with the app, including existing closet items, shopping preferences, as well as their calendar, travel, and purchasing behavior. It’s also building out a business-to-business, CRM-type system for private stylists and luxury clienteling systems, aiming to bring “structure and continuity to what has traditionally been a fragmented, relationship-driven space”.

Funding and round: $5.5 million, Series A.

Investor(s): A consortium of investors across technology and luxury-adjacent family offices.

Company description: Ruka Hair was founded in 2021 by Tendai Moyo and Ugo Agbai, with the mission of supplying hair extensions that are safe, ethical, and good quality. The brand has now received $4.5 million in funding led by Henkel Ventures, the owner of Olaplex and Schwarzkopf. Ruka will be using the investment to scale its business, starting with the launch of US-based operations later this year. The brand has raised $10 million to date and is stocked at Selfridges.

Investor(s): Henkel Ventures, Freedom Trail Capital, Big Issue Invest, Backed VC, Dina Asher-Smith, Knut Alicke, Sophia Dennis, Didier Morais.

Investor comments: “Ruka Hair exemplifies what we look for: founders solving a real problem with genuine commitment, building through community rather than hype,” said Samyr Laine, co-founder and managing partner of Freedom Trail Capital. “Tendai and Ugo built this brand during one of the most challenging periods for consumer businesses, scaled through an authentic community, and are now pioneering biotech innovation that could reshape an entire category.”

Company description: Since founding Anomaly in 2021, Priyanka Chopra Jonas has scaled her haircare brand across North America, the UK, and the Middle East. In the US, the brand is stocked at Target, while in the UK, Superdrug is one of its biggest retailers. Chopra Jonas launched Anomaly with the aim to bring accessibly priced clean and vegan haircare products to the masses. The investment from Reliance will focus on scaling the brand further in India, alongside growing its international presence.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Reliance Retail (portfolio includes: Pahadi Local and Tira).

Investor comments: “Bringing Anomaly into our portfolio marks a strategic step in expanding our basket of new-age, high-growth beauty brands. Anomaly’s strong global positioning, clean formulation, and accessible pricing make it a compelling addition to our ecosystem,” said Isha Ambani, executive director of Reliance Retail Ventures Limited.

Company description: Luxury skincare brand 111Skin was co-founded by husband and wife duo, Dr. Yannis and Eva Alexandridis, in 2012. Their face masks have gone viral since, and in 2025, the brand received a minority investment from Kim Kardashian and Jay Sammons’s private equity firm Skky Partners to help fund its US expansion. Now, the Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) has invested a minority stake that will go toward science-driven innovation.

Funding and round: Minority investment, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): The Estée Lauder Companies (portfolio includes: Le Labo, Jo Malone London, Clinique, La Mer).

Investor comments: “Skincare is entering a new phase, shaped by the convergence of procedures, longevity, and beauty, as consumers increasingly seek products that deliver visible, treatment-inspired results,” said ELC president and CEO Stéphane de La Faverie. “111Skin exemplifies this shift, translating Dr. Alexandrides’s more than 35 years of surgical and aesthetic treatment experience into high-performance skincare inspired by in-clinic treatments and built on clinical insight, next-generation actives, powerful formulas, and proven efficacy.”

Company description: ICCF is a Shanghai and Paris-based premium fashion group that owns Chinese brand Icicle and French brand Carven (acquired in 2018). Kering has acquired a minority stake in ICCF to help develop the former label as part of Kering’s new House of Wonders initiative, which aims to build partnerships that equip emerging luxury houses with strong cultural relevance across markets, categories, and geographies. Icicle will use the funds to expand internationally and into new product categories.

Funding and round: Minority acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Kering (portfolio includes: Gucci, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta).

Investor comments: “This partnership brings together ICCF’s deep understanding of the Chinese luxury ecosystem and cultural landscape with Kering’s longstanding expertise in craftsmanship, operations, and brand development in Europe,” Kering said in a statement. “Through House of Wonders, Kering aims to build long-term value through a disciplined, partnership-driven approach, engaging with brands defined by a distinctive vision, deep authenticity, and global resonance potential.”

Icicle FW26. Photo: Benjamin Cremel/Getty Images

Company description: Grüns is a US-based supplement brand founded in 2023 by Chad Janis, best known for its greens superfood gummy supplement. The brand is digitally-native, with a strong community and a mixed distributed network across retail and direct-to-consumer. The acquisition signals Unilever’s push into the premium wellness category.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever (portfolio includes: Liquid I.V., Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice).

Investor comments: “As a leader and true innovator in the greens supplement category, what sets Grüns apart is its focused portfolio of science-backed products that people genuinely enjoy, trust, and consistently use,” Jostein Solheim, Unilever Wellbeing CEO, said. “This combination of efficacy and experience is powerful, and together we see a significant opportunity to scale the brand within our wellbeing business.”

Investor(s): Softbank, Andreessen Horowitz, D. E. Shaw Ventures, MGX, TPG, Amazon, Nvidia, Microsoft, BlackRock, Sequoia Capital, and more.

Company description: Whoop is a wearable tech company known for its fitness tracker that analyzes sleep, recovery, and performance. The company has raised $575 million at a $10.1 billion valuation, and aims to invest the funds into expanding globally, particularly in the US, Europe, the Gulf region, Latin America, and Asia.

Funding and round: $575 million, Series G.

Investor(s): Collaborative Fund (portfolio includes: Reddit, Lyft, TaskRabbit), 2PointZero Group, Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), Mubadala Investment Company, Abbott, Mayo Clinic, Cristiano Ronaldo, LeBron James, Rory McIlroy, Niall Horan.

Investor comments: “Whoop has become one of the most important tools I use to support my long-term health,” said Ronaldo in a statement. “I am proud to participate in this round because I believe in the future we are building together. No other company has created a health platform this powerful that people are proud to wear.”

Company description: Enkei is a Stockholm-based circular material startup founded by CEO Lovisa Sunnerholm (ex-Google and Electrolux) and creative director Miriam Bichsel (a former fashion PR who worked with Hermès and Bottega Veneta). The company has developed ReCeramix™, a circular material made from 90% construction and demolition waste that can be used for architectural surfaces and interior applications, replacing concrete, marble, and terrazzo. With the pre-seed funding, the company will invest in research and development and commercialization opportunities.

Investor(s): Redcap Ventures (portfolio includes: Done, Goodfeed, Eatit), Danish architect Anders Lendager, Lendager Group founder Christina Åqvist, Vinning co-founder and former Tarkett CEO Ulf Mattsson, retail exec Fabian Månsson, bio-materials professor Thomas Granfeldt, materials scientist Daniel Strömberg.

Investor comments: “What Enkei has done in less than two years is what the industry has been talking about for decades. The future of architecture depends on how we rethink materials. Solutions that transform waste into high-value building materials are exactly what the construction industry needs if we want to move toward truly circular buildings,” said Lendager.

Company description: Olaplex was founded in 2014 as a salon-first prestige haircare brand. Slowly becoming the poster child for bond-building hair products, Olaplex has spent recent years navigating slowing sales, as well as legal and consumer scrutiny — including a 2023 lawsuit (which has since been dismissed and disputed) alleging a link between its products and hair loss, scalp irritation, and brittle strands.

Funding and round: Acquisition, $1.4 billion.

Company description: Former professional snowboarder Nima Jalali founded Salt & Stone, a Los Angeles-based premium body care in 2017. The brand has rapidly grown with its minimal packaging and products ranging from deodorants, body wash and oils to facial cleansers and candles. Salt & Stone’s distribution is a growing one as it counts Sephora, Healf, Amazon and Space NK as retail partners. Vogue Business first reported the possibility of a Salt & Stone acquisition back in January.

Funding and round: Majority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor comments: “We are thrilled for the opportunity to partner with Salt & Stone, a truly exceptional brand that stands apart in the premium body care and wellness space for its ability to blend experience, performance, and a compelling brand aesthetic,” said ​​David Paresky, a director at Advent. “Nima and the Salt & Stone team have built something rare – a brand with deep consumer loyalty, outstanding products, and an authentic purpose that resonates with today’s consumer all around the world.”

Salt & Stone. Photo: Courtesy of Salt & Stone.

Company description: Huel was founded in 2015 by British entrepreneur Julian Hearn and nutritionist James Collier. Known for its nutritionally complete plant-based meal replacement shakes, Huel hopes to use the investment to expand its position in the competitive supplements category.

Funding and round: Acquisition, €1 billion.

Investor(s): Dandone (portfolio includes: Alpro, Activia, Evian).

Investor comments: “Combining [Huel’s] range and best-in-class digital capabilities with Danone’s global reach and deep nutritional expertise offers exciting opportunities into the new and fast-growing nutritionally complete space, in line with our Renew Danone strategy,” said Dandone CEO Antoine de Saint-Affrique in a statement. “We look forward to learning from one another and unlocking new opportunities and growth for both businesses.”

Company description: Founded in 2020 by Karlee Zhang and Omer Ozener, Hello Klean is a water filtration brand known for its detachable shower heads. The company generated $14.7 million in revenue in 2025, and is projecting $27 million for 2026. Water filter manufacturer Brita has invested a minority investment, with the option to purchase a majority stake over time. Hello Klean plans to use the funds for further product development.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Brita (portfolio includes: Brita, Vivreau, Larq).

Company description: Saks Global has received approval of its five-year business plan by an ad hoc group of the Company’s senior secured bondholders, and has secured access to an additional $300 million of its $1.75 billion in committed capital accordingly. This will provide the company with sufficient liquidity to continue to support operations.

Funding and round: Saks has secured access to an additional $300 million of its $1.75 billion in committed capital.

Company description: Quince, the direct-to-consumer brand that bills itself as a high-quality, accessible alternative for fashion and beyond, has announced a $500 million funding round, resulting in a post-money valuation of $10.1 billion. The funding will support the continued growth and global expansion of Quince’s manufacturer-to-consumer (M2C) operating system, per the release.

Funding and round: $500 million, Series E

Investor(s): ICONIQ (portfolio includes: Oura, Uber, Warby Parker, Zoom), with participation from Baillie Gifford, Basis Set Ventures, DST Global, Marcy Venture Partners, Notable Capital, Wellington Management and WndrCo.

Investor comments: “Quince has built hyperefficient infrastructure that enables it to deliver unmatched value to consumers at scale and, in turn, has built a brand people love,” Yoonkee Sull, general partner at ICONIQ, said in a statement. “By redesigning how premium products are manufactured and delivered, compressing traditional retail cycle times and reducing waste, and building a deep understanding of what customers want in real-time, the company is correcting structural inefficiencies that have long defined retail economics. We are excited to triple down in Quince following a year of strong execution by the team and believe the platform is positioned for durable, long-term growth.”

Company description: Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) has taken full ownership of Forest Essentials, the cosmetics, skincare, and fragrance brand known for its ayurvedic products. The beauty giant took out a minority stake in 2008, before increasing its investment in 2020 to 49%. It marks the first M&A move made by ELC CEO Stéphane de La Faverie, with a full takeover of Forest Essentials expected to close in the second half of 2026.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Estée Lauder Companies (portfolio includes: Jo Malone London, Le Labo, Tom Ford Beauty, and more).

Investor comments: “Today marks a meaningful new chapter in a partnership built over the past 18 years on a foundation of mutual trust and respect. Forest Essentials is an exceptional brand, beloved in India, and created and nurtured by its founder Mira Kulkarni,” said de La Faverie. “We are honored to strengthen our partnership with Mira, who, like Mrs. Estée Lauder, has elevated the prestige beauty industry through a clear vision of authenticity and purpose.”

Company description: MA+Group was founded in 1999 by brothers Massimiliano and Michelangelo Di Battista in 1999 as an artist management agency, which has since expanded with a production arm. The group has now joined The Independents group of agencies to offer its services on a broader geographical scale and to a wider network of clients, the company said.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): The Independents (portfolio includes: Karla Otto, Lucien Pagès, Lefty)

Investor comments: “[MA+Group’s] distinctive portfolio with expertise across artist management, strategy, visual communication and content production creates immediate and natural synergies within The Independents,” said The Independents co-founder and CEO Isabelle Chouvet. “As demand grows for new content and entertainment formats, we are excited to expand our capabilities across artist management and content production, bringing even greater creativity and depth to our integrated global offering.”

Company description: Sleep tech company Eight Sleep, known for its temperature-controlling mattresses covers, is now valued at $1.5 billion after a $50 million round led by Tether Ventures. Now, the company plans to invest the capital in scaling R&D to accelerate predictive model development, expanding clinical trials and regulatory pathways, and deepening global commercial partnerships.

Funding and round: $50 million, strategic round.

Investor(s): Tether Ventures (portfolio includes: Bitdeer, Rumble, Sorted)
