#6644. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6643. Past and Prologue: Burberry’s Daniel Lee is Bringing Fashion—and His Extended Family—Home.

Daniel Lee must be considering the notion of home a lot these days. Not just his 17th-century country house in his native Yorkshire, which he bought last year, but his London place, on a leafy 19th-century square, where he has lived for the last five years. Lee, Burberry’s chief creative officer, is enjoying a reprieve from having repair professionals in—the AC has been on the blink, the underfloor heating went awry, and he has already endured one soul-destroying flood. On this hot July morning, he has sequestered himself in the basement, decorated with a beige sectional sofa and a Gary Hume painting, Greenness Is a Kind of Grief. The room looks onto the garden, and Lee has taken to lying out on a lounger; by adjusting its angle and that of the television, he can watch soccer from outside.

“My social life is watching the match on TV; it’s a bit sad, isn’t it?” Lee says in a soft voice accented by dry humor. “I love all sport—Wimbledon’s great—but I prefer the energy of a football match to a tennis match. Tennis is very polite. People lose themselves at football—it’s like a cult, isn’t it?” I didn’t have Lee down as a sports fanatic, but he seems to revere footballers as much as the likes of Skepta and Olivia Colman, whom he loves collaborating with. (Lee supports Arsenal.) There’s also his daily 8 a.m. gym sessions before work. “The bench press is nice, because you can just lie there,” he says, laughing. “I don’t love cardio anymore—it hurts my knees.”

From left: Edie Campbell wears silk poplin trench coat and sequined georgette dress. Alva Claire wears map-print nylon sateen trench coat. Clothes and accessories (throughout), Burberry.

Lee, 40, tells me this as we sit in his garden, the first of our several meetings. In person, Lee is candid, funny, and thoughtful. “Daniel appreciates realness—and openness,” says Skepta. “And he has the best eye. I’d pretty much wear everything he makes.”

Appointed Burberry’s chief creative officer in 2022, Lee has taken the 170-year-old British brand from his highly conceptual debut, all electric-blue blanket checks and graphic red-rose prints, to his more recent collections, widely praised as much for their cool, considered functionality as for the cut and thrust of their forward direction. (Lee has also seen the brand reach pretax profits of over $65 million in 2026, up from an almost $88 million loss last year.) He came to Burberry after three years at Bottega Veneta—an era that flared up like a firework thanks to the success of the Cassette bag and Lido sandals, with Lee quitting before the spark extinguished itself. Before that: six years with Phoebe Philo at Celine, eventually becoming her design director; and before that Donna Karan in New York, following internships at Maison Margiela and Nicolas Ghesquière–era Balenciaga after his graduation from Central Saint Martins.

While the CV reads like a conceptualist designer’s dream, Lee’s Burberry role may be the most reflective of who he really is: pragmatic, unpretentious, driven by a sense of purpose. For his friend Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who has known him since Bottega Veneta, Lee the person and the designer are one and the same. “The reason I feel so at ease in Daniel’s company is that he is grounded and down-to-earth,” she says. “He has this incredible talent and work ethic, yet there’s no pretense with him, no drama.”

From left: Romeo Beckham wears silk shirt, silk scarf, leather trousers, belt, and biker boots. Simone Ashley wears embellished satin dress, leather shoes, and frame bag. Paapa Essiedu wears nylon sateen trench coat, silk shirt, wool trousers, and leather shoes.

When he started at Burberry, Lee says, “it took me a minute to adjust. What I did in the past was about the dream [of fashion], and it was the accessories that were the focus. The clothes here are still the dream, yet they’re wearable and useful, not just for a show. Designing Burberry makes you question and consider everything.” He sees himself as “a making designer,” he says. “I enjoy being in the moment and working with instinct, with craft, with my hands—the physicality of that.”

Lee’s love of making comes from his family—his father Ian and mother Jenny, his brother Richard and sister Sophie. (Daniel is the eldest.) Ian was a mechanic before he retired, and he now lives in Lee’s Yorkshire home, which is not far from Bradford, where Lee was born and raised. He’s set up a workshop at the back of the house to renovate motorcycles, a lifelong passion, which delights his son to no end—when he and his brother were kids, they would ride the bikes in a field at the back of their house. His mom was the creative one. “She was always making—sewing curtains and baking fancy birthday cakes; she made a Noah’s ark for us, and she even made my aunt, who had a cleaning business, a vacuum cleaner,” Lee says. “It made me think, I just want a job where I can make things.”

Simone wears leather shirt, pleated leather skirt, boots, and bag.

Curtains that Lee’s mom sewed for the family living room now hang in one of the bedrooms at his house in Yorkshire, although “his” is a bit of a misnomer: Lee sees the place as his whole family’s home. The impetus to find somewhere in the area came in the aftermath of his mom’s death just before Christmas 2024. “In those moments,” Lee says, “the creative element of work was soothing—it was like therapy.” He hadn’t even been thinking about getting a place up north, but the undertow of emotion carried him there. His brother and sister-in-law, who live locally, were looking to buy a new home. Lee joined the hunt, and the house he ended up taking was the first and only one he saw. “Before that, I’d always had this quest to live abroad, work abroad, see the world,” he says. “When you’re young, you feel like you’ve got endless time—[then] you realize that, actually, time is finite. My family’s not going to be around forever. I want to spend more time with them.” (One area where Lee would rather keep his private life private is when it comes to dating, though he readily says that he’d like to start his own family: “I would love to have children.”)

His aunt Debbie, his mom’s sister, has moved next door to the 1680s house. It was Debbie who brought Lee to London for the first time when he was 12—they saw the London Eye, took in The Lion King, and ate at the then hip restaurant Sketch. “My aunt was being trendy,” Lee says, laughing affectionately. “She also took me to Harvey Nichols in Leeds. I wasn’t a kid growing up reading Vogue, but looking at the amazing windows at Harvey Nichols and seeing the clothes—that’s when I started to think about fashion.” His grandparents would take him to the Alhambra Theatre in Bradford to see the likes of Chicago (his grandmother’s favorite), which ignited a lifelong love of theater. (On a recent trip to New York, he caught the much-lauded revival of The Rocky Horror Show.)

While Lee’s family has always attended his Burberry runway shows, in the weeks and months after his mom’s death, the closeness deepened. His grandmother came to the show in February 2025 with a photograph of Lee’s mom in her handbag, and it was she who sat with him the night before the presentation as he worked on the last of the fittings. His sister, meanwhile, wore the Bur­berry trench that had been their mom’s. “She wore it to my first show,” Lee recalls.

“One thing about Daniel is that he has never forgotten his roots,” says Lee’s father, “and I think that’s why Yorkshire will always feel like home to him.” That feeling of reconnection is something to which Lee has given a lot of thought. “That’s the real value of the North [for me],” he says. “It gives you a sense of shared ownership of the difficult times, which makes things easier.”

Burberry’s headquarters are on Horseferry Road in London, walking distance from both Buckingham Palace and Tate Britain. Lee’s office and studio are on the seventh floor. He designs Tuesday to Thursday, reserving Monday and Friday for prep days—so the team, he says, can have their weekends free of work. Lee likes to be efficient—the late Virgil Abloh told him that creative directors shouldn’t waste their time emailing, so he doesn’t: He and his team speak constantly via WhatsApp instead.

In one corner of the vast workroom, Burberry archivist Carly Eck has assembled a rail of pieces taken from the 25,000 that the company holds—including the earliest trench, dating from 1917—with an eye to what Lee has responded to: the 1930s Highlander cape, with straps to allow freedom of movement; a motoring overall that Lee riffed on for his fall 2024 collection; and a coat worn by explorer Ernest Shackleton, which Lee also referenced in 2023. Eck and Lee get together at the beginning of every season to help build narratives connecting Burberry past and present. Lee’s intense curiosity has certainly paid unexpected dividends. The ridiculously cute duck hats that he included in his Burberry debut were inspired by drawings in one of the brand’s catalogs circa 1930s, laid out on a table nearby.

“What we do,” Lee says, “is try to provide people with answers about how to live the best possible way. We make clothes to protect people, to make them feel good, ready, sophisticated. I think the fashion is secondary. The design here starts from a place of utility, functionality, practicality—it has to work before it has to be, let’s say, decorative.” His Burberry collections thus far have variously offered blanket-lined parkas, battalion jackets, long kilts, jaunty capelets, and dandyish suiting; what model and equestrian Edie Campbell, who has worked with Burberry since she was 15 (“I still had braces!”), calls “very wearable, but with an edge. It’s joyful, and there’s a lightness and a playfulness to it.” Accessories—the ka-ching! successes for any fashion brand—are on his mind, even if a star hasn’t quite emerged yet.

But if the past is in the room, so is the future. Burberry’s spring 2027 collection, which he showed in September at Chelsea College of Arts—Jodie Turner-Smith, Jonathan Bailey, and Fiona Shaw on the front row; Central Cee on the catwalk—features trenches both diaphanous and etched with embroidery, as well as rendered in leather that’s been lavishly traced with beading; utilitarian cotton drill mixed with sequins; floral blousons and skirts worn with earthy, low-heeled buckled mules; and jewel-like high slingback shoes made a little less precious by being paired with slouchy socks. One thing always on Lee’s mind: making Burberry speak more to women. “The brand is born out of menswear, and the trenches are a very masculine thing,” he says. “We’re always trying to bring more femininity to it.”

Edie wears silk poplin jacket with shearling trim, sequined jersey dress, and leather shoes.

Color is one way into that, and it’s something that Lee has decisively brought to the brand from the very beginning with what he describes as softer, moorland tones; spring 2027, meanwhile, sings with shades of dusky pink, aubergine, duck-egg blue, and a soft-sunny yellow, reflecting the casual, lived-in feel that he wanted to impart on the clothes. Gary Hume, the painter, recalls meeting Lee when they began working on a Burberry project in 2024. Walking around Hume’s studio, they’d touch the art, communing with it. Having now worked with Lee, the artist feels that the designer’s use of color “doesn’t feel like it’s added on—it’s entirely integral to what Daniel does.”

For spring 2027, Lee also worked with the celebrated octogenarian print designer Celia Birtwell, an intrinsic part of the creative explosion in British art and design in the 1960s, along with her husband, designer Ossie Clark, and David Hockney, her close friend. Lee had gone to see the recent Hockney exhibition at the Serpentine Galleries in London—he feels a strong affinity with the Bradford-born artist, who died in June—and a gingham tablecloth that Hockney used as a leitmotif sparked an idea to collaborate with Birtwell, who created a check with a painterly feel to it and some rather charming vintage-wallpaper floral prints. They feel organic and fresh, a million miles away from CAD—or AI. “Celia brings a human hand, an emotional hand, to something,” Lee says, thrilled by what she has done. “We have an incredible archive, but sometimes it’s exciting to see new things.”

From left: Alva wears mohair/silk shawl coat and chevron-knit dress. Romeo wears leather jacket with shearling collar, silk shirt, flocked jeans, and belt.

Lee and I are to meet for the last time at the Regency Café near the Bur­berry headquarters. Founded in 1946, it hasn’t changed much since, still a haven of egg and chips, Formica, and tea so wonderfully strong you could stand a teaspoon up in it. In its own way, the café’s story isn’t so different from Burberry’s: halcyon Britain, yet a Britishness of global fascination. Seated among the Regency regulars are hordes of creatively dressed kids from all around the world Instagramming their full English breakfasts—the very kind of young, style-conscious types who Burberry would want to attract, though not only them, of course. It is an egalitarian brand, as much for the aristo in a beaten-up trench driving a Land Rover as it is for the bloke on the football terraces.

Pride in Britishness is, after all, intrinsic to Burberry. “It stands for heritage and culture, and all the things and all the people that those mean,” says model Alva Claire, and Lee seconds the thought. “We are the most famous British luxury brand,” he says, “but in a way we’re bigger than fashion: We are a British institution. We’re there to celebrate the best of Britain—great creativity and also great locations.” Lee recounts how so many of his Burberry shoots have been deliberately located outside of London—Skye, Somerset, Norfolk, the Lake District—and he readily agrees (while acknowledging the importance of London Fashion Week to Burberry) that it would be great to show somewhere else in the UK. But where? “Chanel did Manchester…,” I say; “Dior did Scotland,” he adds.

Lee on the winding, cobbled streets of Haworth, in West Yorkshire.

Right now, though, Lee is thinking about 170 years’ worth of moments. The anniversary is, he says, “always on our minds. How do we do it justice? We have been ambitious this year.” Indeed: As well as a monthslong campaign photographing 170 people all over the world wearing Burberry, a special exhibition, “The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon,” is at the V&A ahead of the company’s funding of the museum’s new costume wing, opening in 2028; another Burberry exhibition, “Ever Forward: The Archive On Stage,” opens this month in Shanghai.

Anyone would be asking themselves what’s left to do—and for Lee, there’s plenty. Top of mind for him, professionally, is transforming the brand’s retail environments for its 413 outposts around the world. Personally? Well, he wouldn’t mind, at some point in his life, living in a hot country. Yet he’s not in any rush. He wants progress to be measured and meaningful; to take it in stride. “I mean,” he says, smiling, “I really feel quite content.”

In this story: Hair, Mari Ohashi; makeup, Siobhan Furlong; grooming, Quelle Bester; manicurist, Robbie Tomkins; tailor, Della George.

#6642. Copycat Coopers Hawk Red Wine–Braised Short Ribs

This copycat Cooper's Hawk red wine-braised short ribs recipe delivers fall-apart-tender short ribs bathed in a luxurious sauce. It's like dining out in your kitchen.

One taste of the red wine–braised short ribs at Cooper’s Hawk is enough to understand why they’ve remained a bestseller. A generous portion of melt-in-your-mouth braised short ribs is stacked over a mound of buttery whipped potatoes, then drizzled with umami-rich braising liquid. When served with roasted vegetables and garnished with crispy fried onion strings, it’s a plate of comfort food that’s just as much a feast for the eyes as it is for the taste buds.

Whether you’ve been to Cooper’s Hawk and want to recreate the magic at home, or you don’t live near a Cooper’s Hawk location and want to know what all the fuss is about, this copycat recipe belongs on your must-try list. It’s the perfect recipe for chilly days when you want a meal that feels like a warm hug. It’s also impressive-looking and great for feeding a crowd, so keep it in mind as the holiday season approaches.

Cooper’s Hawk Winery and Restaurant is something like a more refined Cheesecake Factory that’s known for its wine rather than its cheesecake. Let me break it down. First, each chain greets diners by showcasing its specialties: Where the Cheesecake Factory has cases of cheesecake, Cooper’s Hawk has a well-appointed wine shop. Second, both are known for extensive menus that span a wide range of global influences and cuisines. Finally, both have a long list of signature dishes (we’ve replicated many Cheesecake Factory copycat recipes over the years) that keep customers coming back. These copycat Cooper’s Hawk red wine–braised short ribs, for example, are an ode to the dish that’s been on the menu since the restaurant opened its very first location in 2005.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. Sprinkle the short ribs with salt and pepper. In an ovenproof Dutch oven over medium-high heat, brown the ribs in oil in batches. Remove the meat and set it aside.

Add the celery, carrot and onion to the drippings, and cook them until they’re tender. Add the garlic, and cook for one minute longer. Add the wine and broth, stirring to loosen the browned bits from the pan.

Return the ribs to the pot. Add the parsley and thyme. Cover the pot and transfer it to the preheated oven. Cook the ribs for 2 hours to 2 hours and 30 minutes or until the meat is tender.

While the ribs are braising, in a small bowl, whisk all the butter ingredients until they’re blended. Transfer the mixture to a sheet of storage wrap, and roll it into a log. Refrigerate the butter until it’s chilled. Unwrap and slice it.

Place the hot mashed potatoes on a serving plate. Top them with the short ribs. Immediately top the ribs with a slice of Dijon butter and french-fried onions. Garnish the dish with additional fresh parsley, if desired.

Store any leftover short ribs in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Enjoy them within four days. Leftovers can be microwaved in a microwave-safe container, or they can be transferred to a Dutch oven and warmed in a 350° oven until they’re heated through.

Braised short ribs freeze like a dream. Store them in a freezer-safe airtight container and freeze them for three to four months. Defrost them completely in the refrigerator before warming them in the microwave or in the oven.

Short ribs are a heavily marbled cut of beef from the lower portion of the rib cage (the same area as the chuck and brisket). They have a robust, beefy flavor but contain a lot of connective tissue, so you need to cook them slowly with low heat for the meat to become tender.

Braising is one of the best (and most popular) ways to prepare short ribs. That said, you can make bone-in short ribs in a slow cooker or on a wood, pellet or charcoal smoker. To speed up the process, you can also make tender bone-in short ribs in a pressure cooker.

Cooper’s Hawk serves their short ribs with mashed potatoes and roasted vegetables, but that is far from the only pairing option. Serve them over a bowl of creamy polenta or on a bed of buttered egg noodles (similar to beef Stroganoff). For freshness, add a garden salad, grilled asparagus or creamed spinach for a more indulgent spin.

Sure! If you want to recreate Cooper’s Hawk braised short rib risotto, prepare this recipe as directed, minus the potatoes, veggies, and onion strings. Instead, saute a blend of mushrooms in a skillet and prepare this parmesan risotto while the short ribs braise in the oven. When everything is ready, shred the short ribs into small pieces and combine them with the mushrooms and risotto. Serve the risotto in shallow bowls with a few spoonfuls of braising liquid and a drizzle of white truffle oil.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

#6640. The Miami Heat Dropped Brand-New Jerseys Just in Time For Grand Theft Auto VI

Growing up in Oakland, Miami Heat forward Keshad Johnson and his brother Kenny used to sneak away from their parents to play Grand Theft Auto. “It caused some fights between me and him on turns,” Johnson says. “We used to play that if you crash the car, you gotta pass the sticks.”

For many of us who came of age in the early aughts, sneaking away from our parents to play GTA was a rite of passage. And since the first edition of the game dropped in 1997, at least part of the thrill of this fictional world was often tied to the clandestine affair. But next week, Johnson won’t be hiding from anybody. Instead, he’ll be part of a once-in-a-lifetime Grand Theft Auto experience when he and his Heat teammates take the court in special-edition Vice City jerseys inspired by the game.

Grand Theft Auto VI, Vice City, launches on November 19th. But the night before, when the Heat and superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo take on his former team, the Milwaukee Bucks, they'll be ringing in what is by most accounts the biggest video game launch of all time with a special event that only Rockstar Games and the Heat could pull off. “My whole family is trying to get a Vice City jersey,” Johnson said when we spoke last weekend.

“We're bringing sports and entertainment together in a way that's never been done,” adds Miami Heat Chief Creative Officer Jennifer Alvarez. “And we're going to deliver an experience that no one has actually had at an NBA game.”

More on that in a second. But let’s start with the kits: all black, with bright pink accents that pop like neon signs in the South Beach sky. The word “Heat” is splashed across the front. “It's kind of like the outlaw type vibe,” Johnson said. “That's what we want to give when we're on the court.”

Hidden inside the letters and jersey numbers is a map of Miami streets. They were designed by Nike and Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack, whose logos are featured on the jersey and shorts. As the whole campaign makes clear, details matter.

“I feel like Vice City has its own fashion culture,” says Heat star Bam Adebayo.

The jerseys will be available for purchase on game night at the arena, where fans will be transported into the video game itself upon entering the Kaseya Center, whose plaza will be made over with a light-blue Ferrari and turquoise Chevrolet Monte Carlo, just two of the sports cars one can drive in GTA.

A sign hoisted atop the arena will read “Welcome to Vice City.” In fact, Mitchell was late to practice one day because his usual route was blocked by a helicopter that’d been deployed to help install it. “It shows how much time and effort they're trying to put into this new game,” Mitchell says. “This is probably gonna be the greatest game of all time.”

Though everyone involved has kept tight-lipped about what happens once inside the arena, fans attending Heat games have already been able to order burgers from Burger Shot and chicken from Cluckin' Bell, two fictional fast-food chains in the Grand Theft Auto universe. “It's a full 360 experience. I can't wait for people to really understand what that means,” Alvarez said, coyly. “And that's all I can say about it.”

One can understand the secrecy, since the Heat’s Vice City takeover has been two years in the making. It all started when Rockstar Games dropped the trailer for Vice City in December 2023. A digital Kaseya Center can be seen in the first 30 seconds.

“When we saw that we were in the trailer, we thought we should figure something out,” Alvarez recalls. “Because we've been synonymous with the word Vice since 2017."

The Heat launched the Miami Vice campaign in 2017 with its acclaimed Original Vice jerseys that set the standard for NBA teams launching City Edition jerseys. Those campaigns went beyond the uniforms and included local activations like custom license plates and a fashion line created in collaboration with local artists. Over the years, the Heat launched five separate Vice jerseys, each campaign expanding on previous ones. Ask those with the Heat, and they’d agree that this latest installment is the biggest one yet. “It feels like all of it built up to this,” Alvarez said.

To be clear, the Heat don’t look at this as an extension of their own Vice line. Rather, this is meant to be as exclusive as any streetwear brand launch. Also, it’s not easy to transport fans into a video game every single night. Go big, then go home.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has infiltrated Miami, turning the city that inspired Vice City into Vice City itself. Burger Shot came to life through a collaboration with Skinny Louie, a local smash-burger joint that has rebranded their brick-and-mortar (and arena) locations for the launch. Rockstar Games has activations throughout the city, including in Downtown, Little Haiti and the famous Wynwood Walls. It’s an Inception-style, video game outside the video game-type thing that crescendos with the Heat game on the eve of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch.

Players got their first look at the jerseys and the campaign during a team meeting in early October. After hours of presentations about business operations, media responsibilities and other team matters, the energy in the room sparked when Alvarez took the microphone and showed the first Vice City slide. The players locked in. A few even stood up and cheered.

Mitchell, for his part, was taken back to his childhood, when he would come home from his grandma’s house and play Grand Theft Auto until it was time for bed. For a while, Mitchell became obsessed, playing GTA while other popular games like Call of Duty and NBA 2K collected dust.

“I just played that all the time, doing missions, but also just running around,” he remembers. “It's kind of like your own world in a way.”

And next week, he’ll get to enter it IRL.

#6639. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6638. Cranberry and Brie Stuffed Chicken

With its savory spinach filling, fruity sauce and gooey cheese topping, this cranberry Brie chicken makes any day a celebration.

Who doesn’t love a recipe that looks like it took hours in the kitchen, but is actually surprisingly easy to pull off? Our Test Kitchen’s cranberry Brie chicken is one of those impressive dinners. Tender chicken breasts are stuffed with a spinach filling, coated in bread crumbs and baked until golden. Then comes the best part: the cranberry sauce topping and slices of creamy Brie that melt right over the top.

With its festive colors and a blend of sweet and savory flavors, this dish is a great choice for Friendsgiving, Christmas Eve dinner or any occasion you want to impress guests. But don’t save it just for company! It’s also a fun way to dress up chicken breasts during the week.

Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a large skillet, cook the onion in oil until it’s almost tender. Add the spinach and garlic, and cook them until the spinach is wilted. Drain any liquid, if necessary. Season the filling with salt and pepper.

Pound the chicken breasts with a meat mallet to 1/4-inch thickness. Divide the spinach mixture among the pieces. Fold the chicken breasts in half, enclosing the filling, and secure them with toothpicks.

Place the bread crumbs and egg in separate shallow bowls. Dip the stuffed chicken breasts into the egg, then roll them in the crumbs to coat them. Place them seam side down in an 8-inch square baking dish coated with cooking spray. Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 25 minutes.

Spoon the cranberry sauce over the stuffed chicken breasts. Top them with slices of Brie (if desired, remove the rind from the Brie). Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 10 to 15 minutes longer or until a thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 165°. Discard the toothpicks before serving the chicken. If desired, garnish it with rosemary sprigs.

Let leftover cranberry Brie chicken cool slightly, then transfer it to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to four days. The breading will soften as it sits, especially under the cranberry sauce and melted Brie, but it’ll still be tasty once reheated.

Cranberry Brie chicken tastes best fresh out of the oven, but you can absolutely get a head start on prepping the recipe. Make the spinach filling, and stuff the chicken breasts, securing them with toothpicks. Cover and refrigerate both for up to 24 hours.

When you’re ready to make dinner, dip the chicken in the egg, coat it with bread crumbs and bake it as directed. Save the cranberry sauce and Brie for the last 10 to 15 minutes of baking. Waiting to coat the chicken until just before baking helps keep the bread crumbs from getting soggy.

Reheat cranberry Brie chicken, loosely covered with foil, in a 350° oven until it’s warmed through to 165°. The microwave also works for single servings, but the breading will be a little soggier.

We love Brie here because its mild flavor and creamy texture pair so well with the tart cranberry sauce, but it’s not your only option. Camembert has a similar creamy texture and earthy flavor, or you could use goat cheese if you want something bolder and tangier. For a milder, kid-friendly option, try mozzarella or fontina. Both melt beautifully into a gooey, cheesy topping.

Boneless skinless chicken thighs can work in this recipe, but their smaller size makes them a little trickier to pound thin and fold around the spinach filling. If possible, choose larger thighs, and use toothpicks to keep the filling tucked inside. Since thighs vary in size and thickness, you may need to adjust baking time. Use a meat thermometer to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165° before serving it.

Cranberry Brie chicken fits right in with holiday favorites like creamy mashed potatoes, roasted Brussels sprouts, stuffing or green bean casserole. For a more casual weeknight dinner, serve it over hot, fluffy rice to soak up the extra cranberry sauce, or pair it with roasted sweet potatoes or a simple green salad. And you can’t go wrong with a side of crusty bread, warm buttermilk biscuits or cornbread!

#6637. The Health Benefits of Stair Climbing

We’ve all heard the recommendation to “take the stairs” instead of the escalator or elevator. Not only is it an easy way to squeeze more movement into your day, but research has linked stair climbing to better cardiovascular health and longevity. Even the famously long-lived residents of Barbagia, Sardinia—one of the world’s so-called Blue Zones—spend much of their day navigating steep hills and staircases.

But nutritionist Marián García—better known as Boticaria García, author of Mujeres de Hierro (Iron Women)—takes the humble staircase one step further.

According to Garcia, the benefits of climbing stairs are more numerous than many of us realize: the activity can help increase energy expenditure, improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthen muscles and bones, and even blunt post-meal blood sugar spikes—benefits that become especially valuable after 40, when metabolism, muscle mass, and hormone levels begin to shift.

According to García, consistency matters more than intensity. “When I started running, I incorporated stairs on my way home as the finishing touch to my workout,” she writes in Mujeres de Hierro. “Over time, the habit grew, and today I not only seek out stairs wherever I go—whether at work or in hotels—but sometimes I even climb them carrying grocery bags or suitcases.”

You don’t even need to spend hours on the stair climber at the gym to reap the benefits. García’s recommendation is easy to remember: Simply aim to climb three flights of stairs three times a day. The advice comes from a study in which sedentary adults climbed approximately 60 steps—about three flights—at a brisk pace three times a day, three days a week, for six weeks. By the end of the study, participants had significantly improved their cardiovascular fitness.

García recommends aiming for an effort level of around six or seven out of 10. “You should be breathing harder and your legs should know they’re working,” she says. “You don't need to sprint or arrive at the top completely out of breath—but you shouldn’t be climbing while looking at your phone, either.”

Once stair climbing becomes part of your routine, García suggests making two small adjustments.

Take two steps at a time: “Your stride lengthens, and your glutes and legs have to work harder. That muscle contraction also increases the stimulus on the bone,” she explains.

Vary your pace: Alternate between climbing quickly and more slowly rather than maintaining the same rhythm throughout. “Changing the pace increases the demand and prevents your legs from climbing on autopilot,” she explains.

The strategy is based on what’s known as Frost’s mechanostat—the idea that bone adapts to the loads placed upon it. “If bone receives sufficient and varied stimuli, it understands that it needs to stay strong. If we never challenge it, it becomes complacent,” García says.

One of stair climbing’s most surprising benefits has to do with blood sugar. “Stairs are like a mini gym between floors,” García says. “They engage your glutes and legs, get your heart pumping, break up sedentary time, and increase energy expenditure.”

Research has also found that just one minute of stair climbing after a meal can help reduce the post-meal rise in blood glucose. “No, it doesn’t cancel out the pudding for dessert,” García jokes, “but it gets your muscles to remove some of the glucose circulating in your blood.”

Of course, she isn’t suggesting that stair climbing replaces strength training or cardio. Instead, she sees it as something even more valuable: a tiny habit that’s easy to repeat every day. “It’s a small, repeated action that gradually builds up your health savings,” she notes.

#6636. My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them.

By all logic I should be sick of this chicken. I have cooked it, give or take, a hundred times. When I don’t know what to make for dinner—or, honestly, don’t want to make dinner at all—it is there for me, like a gentle friend.

The marinade is deceptively simple: equal parts miso and honey, plus a glug of soy sauce. Nothing more. There’s no gotcha moment, no pepper hiding in plain sight or olive oil I forgot to account for. The flavor excels because each ingredient punches above its weight. Both fermented, the miso and soy sauce add umami depth, while honey supplies sweetness and makes the chicken glossy, like ceramics pulled straight from the kiln.

I’m often deflated when I see the word marinade in a recipe. No, I don’t have time for “at least an hour” or, more likely, the dreaded “preferably overnight.” Don’t they know it’s a Tuesday? This marinade, mercifully, is immediate. Because it is more of a paste than a liquid, you can slather it directly onto the chicken before hurling the baking sheet into the oven. (Of course, if you’re the type of person who has the wherewithal to start meal prep the night before, that works too.)

A short stint under the fierce heat of the broiler transforms the miso coating into a burnished, sticky crust in 15-ish minutes while you work on the rest of the meal. Old-school drawer-style broilers can get a little overexcited, so start peeking in after 10 minutes. Now is not the time to check the mail or start a load of laundry.

This chicken shines with rice tucked underneath, which catches every saucy streak. But you could build it out with roasted vegetables. Sometimes I’ll add oiled-up broccoli or asparagus to the baking sheet. Other times it’s just the chicken, with a shower of scallions if I’m feeling fancy. Then I make it all again next week.

#6635. This Genius Trick Makes Perfectly Portioned Cinnamon Rolls—No Ruler or Guessing Required

This clever little move turns your knife into a measuring guide for cinnamon rolls.

I have no objection to a shortcut in the kitchen. I’m happy to let boxed cake mix handle dessert or a great jar of pasta sauce get dinner moving. But I just can’t make peace with cinnamon rolls from a can. I want to love them. I appreciate the convenience, and I understand the appeal of having warm cinnamon rolls before the coffee is finished brewing. They just never quite satisfy that craving for a warm, deliciously gooey cinnamon roll.

Some viral upgrades make a compelling case—particularly the heavy cream bath and generous additions of butter and brown sugar. But my long-standing love for cinnamon rolls has much more to do with the soft, pillowy dough, so I’m willing to wait through a rise or two.

Having committed to that, though, I’m still interested in anything that makes the process easier. So when I saw a video of someone flipping a knife over a log of cinnamon roll dough to mark perfectly even portions, I wanted to try it. Cutting equal slices by eye can involve a surprising amount of second-guessing when you’d really just like to get them in the pan. I made our classic cinnamon roll recipe and put the trick to the test.

The clever part of this trick is that the knife becomes its own measurement. Rather than judging the thickness of each slice, you use the width of the blade to mark equal portions along the dough roll before slicing it into pieces.

Once your dough is filled and rolled into a log, gently lay the blade flat across the top at one end, with the knife running crosswise over the log. Then flip it onto its opposite flat side, moving along the dough one blade-width at a time. It looks a little like the knife is doing small somersaults, with its edge leaving a light indentation at each turn.

Continue down the log, using just enough pressure to leave visible marks. Then go back and slice through the dough at those marks.

This worked beautifully with our classic cinnamon rolls, but the same technique would work with just about any cinnamon roll recipe. The turning motion was simple, and the knife left an evenly spaced cutting guide along the dough. Once the marks were there, I could slice the rolls without measuring each one or estimating where the next cut should go.

I particularly liked being able to see all the portions before I started cutting. It made the job feel settled: The spacing was already worked out, and all I had to do was follow it. For something that takes so little effort, it’s a useful bit of precision.

This is the kind of cinnamon roll shortcut I can get behind. I still get the homemade rolls I wanted, but there’s one less thing to fuss over before the pan goes into the oven.

#6634. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6633. Tennessee State Representative-Elect Allie Phillips: ‘Living the Struggle Helps Me Understand the Struggle’

It’s pretty remarkable that Allie Phillips answers her own emails, given the mother of two—and newly elected Democratic member of the Tennessee House of Representatives—has been fielding media inquiries nonstop since last week’s midterm elections. In Nashville the weekend after her win, Phillips’s name was still plastered everywhere—from the Honky Tonk Highway entertainment district to the city’s oldest diner to venerable lesbian karaoke institution the Lipstick Lounge.

In an interview conducted over Zoom a few days later, I spoke to the staunch reproductive-rights advocate and self-described “regular, working-class mom” about turning trauma into action, campaigning while pregnant, and hitting the ground running with a full slate of legislative priorities. Read that conversation below.

Vogue: Congratulations! What did election night look like for you?

Allie Phillips: Election night had a pivot in it. I ended up having to leave the watch party for our county party and move over to another location because it was just so full. When I saw the early vote numbers hit, I was about 20% ahead, and within five minutes, a member of the Republican Party in Montgomery County called me and said, “Congratulations, Representative Phillips.” I was like, “None of the precincts have been reported yet,” and he said, “Your opponent would have to take 75% of the Election Day vote, and that’s just not going to happen, so congratulations.” I was like, “I’m going to wait until the last vote is counted, I don’t want to prematurely celebrate.”

I spent the night with amazing organizations like the Equity Alliance Fund, a Black-founded organization that works on expanding Black political engagement, and TIRRC, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition. They contributed to so much of my election-night win—they knocked on over 30,000 doors in my district—so being able to celebrate with them was incredible. When we shifted the watch party to a different location, I stood up on a chair in a restaurant in heels, no podium, no microphone, no media, just me and the people that got me over the finish line, and gave my speech that I wrote. It was probably the most down-to-earth, authentic thing that I think could have happened. I wouldn’t change it for the world, because as stressful as it was to have to pivot in the middle of election night, I did what I needed to do as a leader. It was hectic and chaotic, but we got to celebrate together, and that’s what mattered.

Can you talk about the path that brought you to the Tennessee State House last week?

In 2023, I found out that my pregnancy was incompatible at my anatomy scan. I was almost 20 weeks pregnant, and Tennessee had just recently implemented its near-total abortion ban. Due to my daughter’s conditions, my doctor shared that the longer I stayed pregnant, the worse my health would become. I had a daughter at home already, so I didn’t want to put myself at risk. I had to start looking out-of-state for abortion care, and every state surrounding us is also an abortion-ban state, so we had to go even further.

When you have states like Tennessee and others with abortion bans, you have this influx of out-of-state patients bombarding these clinics that are the closest to them, right? So the wait lists were long. The airfare and travel expenses were costly, so I had to start a GoFundMe online because we couldn’t afford the trip to New York City, where we ended up finding a clinic. I went to that clinic 10 days after my high-risk appointment and found out that my daughter had passed in utero, and my body was not expelling her. The doctor said that because the last confirmed fetal heartbeat was almost two weeks ago, I was now at a greater risk of infections or blood clots or going septic, so essentially, we needed to do the procedure now. Within an hour of finding out that my daughter was gone, I was in a gown going into surgery, and I had to do all that alone. My husband wasn't allowed to be there with me. I’d never been in New York City and didn’t know these doctors from Adam, so that experience was very traumatizing.

Phillips testifying about the lack of reproductive freedom in Tennessee during a Senate Budget Committee hearing in 2024.

When I got back home to Clarksville—after the postpartum black hole that I fell into—I was reached out to by the Center for Reproductive Rights, who asked if I’d be interested in joining a lawsuit against the state of Tennessee that was similar to the one in Texas with [Amanda] Zurawski. I don’t think I’ve said yes to anything quicker in my life. I was like, “Somebody has to do something, because this is atrocious and dehumanizing.” The government made me feel like I was gum under their shoe.

I joined the lawsuit, and now I’m the lead plaintiff in the lawsuit. It’s still ongoing three years later. I have not had the opportunity to testify in a trial because the state keeps moving it, but I knew that would take a while. I knew there wasn’t going to be a decision made by the end of the year, so I went and met with my representative at the time, Jeff Burkhart, and shared with him that I wanted help with the Miley’s Law legislation that I wrote that would give exceptions for fatal fetal anomalies. He said he would help me get it up to the General Assembly, but he never did, and then I got sick and tired of waiting around for him to help me and decided that I would just run against him so I could do it myself.

I had no idea what I was doing. I’d never been involved in politics other than voting, and that was, like, presidential elections. I joined my county party and put my hat in for the race, and I ran a 13-month campaign. We raised over half a million dollars, which is unheard of for a Democrat running in deep red Tennessee for a State House office. I had donations from all 50 states. The news coverage of my race was just insane, and unfortunately we still lost, but I took over 45% of the vote. I was pregnant at the end of that campaign. The first three months of my pregnancy were the most grueling three months of the election, August to November.

Being pregnant in August in Tennessee doesn’t sound easy.

Yeah. It was hot and I was super nauseous and I still had to go out and knock on doors. But I did what I needed to do, and then went off to have my son on April 17, 2025, and was still involved. I was pregnant going to marches and stuff, like, you ain’t stopping me. Then I took a little hiatus for that summer. When I came back to work, I started getting more involved again, and then my opponent [Burkhart] died and there was an appointment to his seat, and so I put my name in for the appointment. Our county commission went through five rounds of voting, ended in a tie between me and Michael Lankford, the Republican, and the mayor gave his deciding vote to Michael Lankford, so Michael Lankford was appointed to the seat. He served this last session, so I ran against him this year. We went from being 45% of the vote in 2024 to taking 55% of the vote this year, which was not what we were anticipating. We thought I might win by a couple of hundred votes, maybe, and I think we took it by about 1,600.

I think it says a lot about the dynamic of voters and where they’re sitting with parties right now, because I can tell you, the majority of those voters were not Democrats. There were independents, there were Republicans, and I think that’s incredible. We really had a message of putting working families first; like, I’m a mom of two, I come to work in Nashville every day, my husband works the night shift because we can’t afford childcare, and we do what we have to do to get by. I’m not some wealthy lawyer or entrepreneur with my own business who’s like, Oh, sure, I can be a lawmaker, too. I’m just a regular working-class mom, and I think people want to see more of that in their government. They saw their families in me. They saw themselves in me. I think that’s what made the difference this time versus in the last election, which was just, Oh, she’s all about abortion. What else is she running on? I was like, “A lot of things!” Nobody wanted to talk about them, though, because everybody wants to talk about my story.

Can you tell me a bit about the district you’re now representing?

I am in District 75, which is the western portion of Clarksville. It’s Montgomery County, and the Tennessee portion of the Fort Campbell military base is in my district. Outside of Clarksville’s city limits, we have a lot of really rural farm areas, and that makes this district really unique because we have so much agriculture, and then you come into Clarksville and it’s kind of urban and suburban, a little bit of both. With it being a military town, people are coming and going all the time, so in a small rural district, you might run for office once and then run again and knock the same doors and meet the same people, but in the four years that I’ve lived in Clarksville, I’ve only had one neighbor stay the same. You have people stationed here for a year, 18 months, six months. The doors I knocked in ’24 who supported me, those people aren’t there anymore. It’s different people. A lot of the people that are here don’t vote here, they vote back home or they don’t register to vote at all because they move so much. Clarksville has a university, Austin Peay State University, that’s not in my district; it's in the district next to mine. But there are college students that live in my district, so it’s a double-edged sword. We love the college and we love the military, but it makes it really difficult to navigate the demographic of the voters because they change so often.

What do you think has most prepared you to hold your current office?

I think it’s the experiences that I’ve been through. I grew up in a lower-income family in the small town of Ashland City in Cheatham County. My dad was a construction worker, my mom went to college to become a paralegal, and we didn’t have a lot of money. Growing up, I was taught, You work for the things you want, period. You don’t ask for handouts. Then I went to school to get a bachelor’s degree in multimedia journalism.

Growing up and watching my parents struggle, and then becoming a mother myself and seeing how difficult it is just to be able to afford formula, food, diapers, toys… Everything my daughter had was handed down to us or found on Facebook Marketplace. The older I got, the more I learned that a lot of this is policy. Our General Assembly has refused to cut the grocery tax. We’re one of 13 states that still has one, and it’s at nine and a half percent. We’re paying more for what? People shouldn’t have to struggle to get access to a healthcare professional to get their medication. That’s a policy decision. They could expand Medicaid, but they won’t. Our roads shouldn’t have potholes every quarter-foot or have you sitting in traffic for three hours a day. We could invest in mass transit, but they won’t. I was a single mom for the first three years of my daughter’s life. I was working three jobs while going to college full-time. So knowing and seeing and living the struggle helps me understand the struggle. I’m not a single mom anymore, but we still struggle. If you don’t live this, you don’t understand it. This is nothing against my opponent [Lankford], but we’re both 31 and he’s not married, he doesn’t have any kids, and he lives on property owned by his family.

Completely. He’s a senior banker or something like that, but has he had to serve tables before and rely on tips to pay his bills? He’s never had to worry about getting his children to daycare so he can get to work, and he’s never had to figure out, Well, my kids are sick, so they can’t go to daycare, and now I’ve got to call out of work. My lived experiences are what made me feel qualified for this, because to be a representative is to represent the people, and I grew up seeing what hard work looks like.

What other races were you excited about or watching closely last Tuesday?

The top three races in Tennessee that we were looking to flip were mine, Jesse Huseth down in Memphis, and Brian Goldberg out in Knoxville. I was really curious to know if they were winning voters, and they did. They flipped their seats, and we flipped three additional seats that we weren’t really honed in on. I was disappointed that Jerri Green didn’t win against Marsha Blackburn, but I’m extremely proud of her for how close she got and the campaign that she ran. I was also disappointed in the congressional races that we were looking at with Justin Pearson, Chaz Mulder, and Darden Copeland, but I was very proud of Victoria Broderick for flipping her seat. That’s why you don’t underestimate women; we just show up out of nowhere sometimes! All in all, I’m fairly happy. We have 11 new Democrats going into the House, and I think the chairman said this is the biggest freshman class since either the ’80s or the ’90s. It’s really exciting for Democrats in the state and hopefully gives people more hope that we will continue moving forward.

What’s first on your docket, legislation-wise?

Well, priority number one is my district, always. But as far as legislation, I mentioned Miley’s Law. Outside of reproductive access, I ran my campaign on affordability for working families, so I would love to carry a bill about cutting the tax on diapers and potentially formula. If we can cut the grocery tax, the formula tax goes away, because formula is taxed with our food percentage. I want to cut property taxes for veterans—they served our country, give them a break—and then there was one about creating a lottery for a Tennessee fund for veterans, specifically, that would give them additional help with finding things like healthcare access, mental healthcare, housing, jobs, whatever it may be. My district is so military-heavy that supporting them is so important to me. I plan to be a strong advocate against school vouchers; I am wholeheartedly for fully funding our public schools. I want to make sure our schools are fully funded and that teachers are paid what they’re worth and kids are eating in school, and that we’re not funding private entities with public dollars.

Last question: How are you celebrating your big win and new role?

There really hasn’t been any opportunity to celebrate. I’m still trying to respond to text messages from election night. [Laughs.] I was put on payroll at midnight after the election, so it’s been go-go-go since, but I can tell you that I’m able to sleep better knowing that I’m not stressed out so much by the election. My oldest daughter, who’s nine, was missing me a lot during the campaign, so she's like, “Do you actually get to be home now?” I was like, “Uh, kind of.” She’s my biggest supporter.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

#6631. The 10 Best Aldi Finds of November Include the Cutest Stocking Stuffer for Little Shoppers

From flavor mash-up snacks and holiday decor to a very special Barbie doll, these November Aldi Finds deserve a spot in your shopping cart.

November is one of my favorite months to go grocery shopping. First, no one can deny that it is peak soup season, so I love stocking up on ingredients for creamy butternut squash soup or a classic lentil stew. I never seem to mind that the sun sets earlier when I have a truly cozy lineup of fall dinner recipes.

And of course, Thanksgiving preparations take up a bulk of the month as well. In my family, I am tasked with two things: bread and Thanksgiving desserts. This year I am going to try my hand at making a sourdough pecan pie! Aldi is definitely the first place I go for my Thanksgiving shopping, because it’s guaranteed to have all my ingredients in stock. And, of course, there’s no shortage of seasonal goodies to look forward to.

Every month, Aldi drops a slew of new items and brings back some customer favorites. Since the grocery store is famous for its motto of “Here today, gone tomorrow,” I’ve turned my passion into an inside scoop so you can stock up while things last. Here are the most exciting November Aldi Finds that will make the holiday season even better.

Nothing says “welcome to the holidays” quite like a big wreath on the front door. This wreath has tiny pine cones and lights, which makes it even more magical. I love that it’s available with either a red or green velvet ribbon, so you can choose which suits your personal aesthetic best.

Of course, if you prefer savory treats over sweet ones, then you might really enjoy these turkey stuffing-flavored potato chips. All the classic Thanksgiving flavors you love, but in chip form. The wavy chip makes it perfect for dipping—say, in some homemade cranberry sauce?

This board is such a great idea! The snowman outline gives you plenty of opportunities to arrange your favorite meats and cheeses in a cute way. The snap-top lid ensures everything stays in place during transit from your house to wherever the party is. It’s so festive, I might just be giving these as gifts this year.

I’m a sucker for any kind of fancy bread, and this loaf in particular caught my eye. Imagine the pillowy sweet softness of a classic brioche, but with added maple nut flavor. It sounds like a breakfast dream come true! I’ll be using this for Thanksgiving leftover sandwiches and French toast.

If there’s one thing Aldi does well, it’s providing exceptionally budget-friendly dupes of much fancier brands. Like this adorable cherry red braiser pan, which has a leaf design on the lid. It might cost upward of $300 from some brands, but Aldi gives it to you at a mere fraction of the price.

OK, this is so cool! A special Aldi-branded Barbie doll is a perfect stocking stuffer for any of the grocery-obsessed kids (or adults!) in your life. This Barbie comes with her own shopping cart and reusable tote, so she is ready to stock up on all her favorite Aldi finds.

I have several holiday runners from Aldi, and they are some of my favorite pieces of decor. This beautiful floral version has big poinsettia flowers and holly leaves, so it’s sure to make a statement on your table for the holidays. It’s machine washable, too, which is very convenient—you don’t need to stress if someone spills red wine on it (speaking from experience!)

This has been my absolute favorite seasonal Aldi find over the last few years. Adding a few of these fancy flavored marshmallows to a simple cup of hot cocoa transforms it into an irresistible treat. I am partial to the peppermint flavor, but the salted caramel marshmallows are also incredible. And again, they are perfect for gifting!

Which Aldi Find are you most excited for this month? Let us know in the comments below!

#6630. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

#6629. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6628. This Coffee Subscription Delivers Some of the Freshest Beans We’ve Tried

It's one of the best gifts you can give to coffee lovers this holiday season.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It really doesn't get fresher than this. A Storyville coffee subscription delivers delicious beans right to your doorstep.

We’ve all been there. Standing in the grocery store staring at dozens of coffee brands and trying to decide which one might perk us up, only to end up scowling at a subpar cup of sludge the next morning. Well, those days are over because Storyville, one of Seattle’s best coffee shops, now delivers freshly roasted beans straight to your door.

I tried a Storyville coffee subscription, and I assure you that you’ll never have to waste your time (or money) on stale beans again. Here’s everything you need to know about this caffeinated club.

Storyville is one of the highest-rated coffee shops in Seattle, with locations at Pike Place and at 1st and Madison. They also have a roasting studio you can tour to see exactly where your coffee beans are roasted before making their way to your door. But if you can’t make it to Seattle, they also offer coffee subscription services with nationwide shipping.

The brand sources premium-grade green coffees and roasts each bean varietal individually before blending. Beans are roasted on the darker end of medium and feature a rich, natural sweetness with notes of chocolate and caramel. Unlike many other dark roasts, this coffee has a smooth finish and no bitterness. Best of all, Storyville ships its coffee immediately after roasting.

Storyville subscriptions are highly customizable in order to fit your needs. First, choose between whole beans and single-serve pods. Then choose the quantity and delivery frequency that best suits your needs. You can pause, skip or cancel via text at any time. Moreover, you’ll receive 20% off, among other perks.

I am a coffee fiend. On any given day, I’m three cups in by 9 a.m. That’s why I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a bag of real Seattle coffee.

My order arrived on Wednesday, October 28. I received a bag of Prologue coffee beans, Sunrise espresso beans and Epilogue decaf coffee beans. I knew the roast dates would be stamped on the bags, but I was amazed to see that my beans had been roasted just days prior, on October 25 and October 27. Talk about fresh!

I opened the Prologue first and poured the entire bag into the bean hopper of my De’Longhi Rivelia. After brewing, I took a sip before adding my cream and sugar and was amazed by how smooth it was. It was fresh and flavorful without a hint of bitterness. I love a dark roast and could drink this all day long.

The next day, I opened the Sunrise espresso beans. I used it to make a regular cup of coffee followed by an Americano. Like the Prologue, the beans were clearly fresh, and the coffee was exceptionally smooth! I’ll be saving this bag along with the decaf for espresso martinis with my girlfriends.

As a dark roast gal, I’ve had my fair share of coffee that tastes bitter or burnt. I didn’t get any notes of bitterness from Storyville coffee. I’ll also point out that a bag of Prologue coffee lasted one week. Given how much coffee I drink plus the fact that my husband tends to make a cup here and there, I’m not surprised we went through it so quickly. Luckily, the subscription is completely customizable. If you drink as much coffee as I do, you’ll want to order two or three bags at a time. But if you just enjoy one cup per day, then one bag at a time will suffice.

That said, these beans are so fresh we wouldn’t be surprised if you start drinking more coffee than usual. And we certainly wouldn’t blame you!

It’s also easy to send a subscription as a gift. Simply head over to their gifting page and opt for three, five, eight or 12 prepaid shipments.

#6627. Baked Feta Bites

Baked feta pasta took the world by storm, and once we tried it, we knew we couldn’t stop at just the classic viral recipe. We created these baked feta bites to be the perfect no-fuss holiday appetizer, capturing all of the same flavors as the OG. Thanks to easy, store-bought ingredients, these flaky, flavor-packed bites are perfect for any last-minute party planning.

The puff pastry:Puff pastry can be a game-changer in appetizer recipes, and selecting the right one is essential. Because your choice of puff pastry determines the overall texture, we recommend opting for as high a quality as you can find. Brands like Taste of Inspirations, Pepperidge Farm, or Dufour offer excellent options that guarantee a delicate, flaky crust that will elevate your bites to a whole new level of perfection.

Speaking of, we understand that achieving flawlessly cut squares can be a daunting task. Here’s a quick guide to ensure your squares are uniform: On a lightly floured surface, roll out the puff pastry sheets, smoothing out any creases. Using a chef’s knife, cut your pastry in half crosswise, then each piece in half crosswise again, so you have 4 strips of pastry. Cut those in half lengthwise, then cut each piece into 3 squares, until you have 24 squares.

How to make baked feta bites:Once you’ve got your pastry squares, you can begin assembling your bites, starting with greasing a mini muffin tin with cooking spray. Gently press each square into the prepared cups, allowing the pastry to protrude slightly—this subtle bump will transform into a beautifully cupped shape during baking. Then add in your dollop of jam, shallots, a piece of roasted red pepper, a cube of feta (crumbled feta is perfectly fine too!), and a touch of thyme. We love these as is, but feel free to switch things up if you like—who knows, you might just discover a new flavor combo you’ll make again and again.

Storage & make ahead:Wondering about leftovers? Worry not. These baked feta bites are just as delightful the next day. Store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator, and when you’re ready for another flavor-packed moment, simply reheat them in the oven to restore their crispiness. Want to make these way ahead of time? Bake these, let them cool, and then place them in a freezer-safe bag before storing in the freezer for up to 3 months.

#6626. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.
